Set-valued mappings and enlargement of monotone operators.

The main aim of this book is to give a relatively brief and self-contained review of the basics of set-valued analysis in a Banach space, and to present most significant results related to existence of fixed points of multivalued mappings. As the title indicates, much attention is paid to convex analysis and to analysis of monotone operators. The book also covers recent trends in these fields and applications to iterative solution methods for fixed point problems and variational inequalities in Banach spaces and in finite dimensional spaces.

Formally, the material of the book can be divided into two parts. In the first part (Chapters 2--4), the authors summarize classical results from set-valued analysis, convex analysis, and the theory of monotone operators. Chapter 2 is dedicated mostly to continuity properties of point-to-set mappings in Banach spaces. Here, among others, Open map theorem and Closed graph theorem for closed convex processes are presented. Chapter 3 contains the basic core of convex analysis, leading to classical fixed point results for set-valued mappings due to Caristi, Ekeland, Ky Fan, and Kakutani. In Chapter 4, the authors introduce and study in detail the central object of investigation in this book, namely, the class of maximal monotone operators. Among key results of the chapter, the Debrunner-Flor theorem on an extension of a monotone set, the Rockafellar theorem on the convexity of the range of a maximal monotone mapping, and theorems on maximal monotonicity of sums of maximal monotone operators should be mentioned. The material of Chapters 2--4 is supplemented with a large variety of exercises. The exercises vary in difficulty from simple technical examples to theoretical propositions amplifying the main text. These chapters can be used for teaching a one-quarter course in set-valued analysis or convex analysis at the MSc or PhD level. The second part (Chapters 5, 6) contains recent results that have not yet been published in monograph literature. Chapter 5 is devoted to enlargements of maximal monotone operators. The most important and well-known example of such an enlargement is the \(\varepsilon\)-subdifferential of a convex function with respect to the standard subdifferential of this function. It is shown that an enlargement can be defined for an arbitrary maximal monotone operator in such a way that it inherits many of useful properties of the \(\varepsilon\)-subdifferential. The results are applied in particular to the justification of set-valued versions of extragradient method for solving finite dimensional variational inequalities. Finally, Chapter 6 applies the developed theory to the proximal point algorithms in Banach and Hilbert spaces. At the end of each chapter the authors give detailed historical notes and references for further reading. The volume can be read by anyone with a basic knowledge of real and functional analysis.

Slamming of ships: where are we now?

Summary: Literature published on the problem of ship slamming in waves is reviewed from the point of view of someone working at a ship research institute. Such an institute is confronted with rather practical questions regarding the acceptability of certain design parameters such as the acceptable amount of bow flare angle for use at sea. The importance of these questions is illustrated by noting that actual slamming or the presumed danger of slamming is the main reason for ship operators to reduce speed or to change heading. The review shows that such questions cannot yet be answered. The problem of the local effect of the impact is very complicated owing to the importance of air inclusions, bubbles in the water, compressibility of water and cavitation effects. Only a computational method properly including all these effects will give an accurate answer; also model tests will not be capable of doing this, if only because the methods to extrapolate the results of models to full scale are not yet developed. The problem of the global response of the ship to a wave impact is closer to being solved. A two-stage approach is proposed, consisting of a computational fluid dynamics method for individual impacts and an approximate method to be included in long-term simulations. However, to arrive at a realistic long-term distribution, one has to account for the seamanship of the captain; avoiding the worst conditions or adapting the ship speed and course has a large effect on the actual extremes. Research on this topic has hardly begun.

Stabilization of coupled systems of quadratic integral equations of Chandrasekhar type

The authors consider the coupled system of integral equations
\[
x(t)=a_1(t)+g_1\big(t,y(t)\big)\int_0^t\frac{t}{t+s}f_1\big(s,y(s)\big)\;ds
\]
and
\[
y(t)=a_2(t)+g_2\big(t,x(t)\big)\int_0^t\frac{t}{t+s}f_2\big(s,x(s)\big)\;ds,
\]
where, in each case, \(t\in[0,b]\). Using the Schauder fixed point theorem, the authors deduce existence of at least one solution to this system. The hypotheses imposed are relatively standard growth and regularity hypotheses on the various maps, but, nonetheless, are too numerous to list here. In addition to the existence theorem, the authors also investigate the so-called asymptotic stability of the system.

Overall, the paper seems to be written mostly clearly, but there are some points that are confusing. First of all, the given MSC codes make no sense, seeing as they are listed as 32A55 and 11D09, which are analytic function theory and number theory, respectively -- topics that have nothing to do with the mathematics at hand. Moreover, while the authors norm the space \(\mathcal{C}(I)\), for \(I\) an interval, in the usual way, namely \(\| y\|:=\max_{t\in I}|y(t)|\), the use of the maximum function only makes sense if \(I\) is compact, which is not mentioned -- though it seems to be assumed that \(I:=[0,b]\) is the default assumption throughout the paper. Furthermore, since the authors operate in the product space \(\mathcal{C}(I)\times\mathcal{C}(I)\), seeing as they are considering a system, it is curious that the authors do not seem to norm this product space, even though calculations involving \(\|(x,y)\|\), for \((x,y)\in\mathcal{C}(I)\times\mathcal{C}(I)\), do arise in the paper. A close reading of the paper seems to suggest that the tacit assumption is that \(\|(x,y)\|:=\max\big\{\| x\|,\| y\|\big\}\), but the reviewer is unsure of this. In any case, the reader is urged to be cautious in his or her reading of this paper since some of the calculations do not seem to be rendered carefully.

Nonetheless, the analysis provided in the paper is interesting. And researchers in the general areas of integral equations or fixed point theory might find this of interest.

Categories of hypermagmas, hypergroups, and related hyperstructures

Hypergroups [\textit{F. Marty}, in: 8. Skand. Mat. Kongr., Stockholm,45--49 (1934; JFM 61.1014.03)] are a generalization of groups that allow for the product of two elements to be a nonempty set of elements, while hyperrings and hyperfields [Zbl 0085.26501, \S 3] are ring-like objects whose additive structure is a particular kind of hypergroup. This paper aims to analyze hypergroups and related structures within a categorical context.

The paper considers the following categories
\[
\begin{array} [c]{ccccccc} \mathsf{cMsc} & \subset & \mathsf{Msc} & \subset & \mathsf{uHMag} & \hookrightarrow & \mathsf{HMag}\\
\cup & & \cup & & \cup & & \\
\mathsf{Can} & \subset & \mathsf{HGrp} & \subset & \mathsf{HMon} & & \\
\cup & & \cup & & \cup & & \\
\mathsf{Ab} & \subset & \mathsf{Grp} & \subset & \mathsf{Mon} & & \end{array}
\]
where

\begin{itemize}
\item \(\mathsf{HMag}\) and \(\mathsf{uHMag}\)\ are the categories of hypermagmas [\textit{A. Dudzik}, ``Quantales and hyperstructures: monads, Mo' problems'', Preprint, \url{arXiv:1707.09227}] and unital hypermagmas;

\item \(\mathsf{Msc}\) and \(\mathsf{cMsc}\)\ are the categories of mosaics and commutative mosaics;

\item \(\mathsf{HGrp}\), \(\mathsf{Can}\)\ and \(\mathsf{HMon}\)\ are the categories of hypergroups, canonical hypergroups and hypermonoids;

\item \(\mathsf{Mon}\), \(\mathsf{Grp}\)\ and \(\mathsf{Ab}\)\ denote the usual categories of monoids, groups and abelian groups.
\end{itemize}

It is shown that the categories \(\mathsf{HMag}\), \(\mathsf{uHMag}\)\ and \(\mathsf{Msc}\) are complete and cocomplete, while the categories of hypergroups and canoical hypergroups fail to be either complete or cocomplete. The various epimorphisms and monomorphisms are characterized in the categories \(\mathsf{HMag}\), \(\mathsf{uHMag}\), \(\mathsf{Msc}\)\ and \(\mathsf{cMsc}\). It turns out that the categories \(\mathsf{HMag}\), \(\mathsf{uHMag}\)\ and \(\mathsf{cMsc}\) are of closed monoidal structures. The following two theorems are established in the final section (\S 4).

Theorem. The categories of multirings and hyperrings have fully faithful embeddings into the category of monoid objects in \(\mathsf{cMsc}\).

Theorem. There is a faithful functor
\[
\mathsf{sMat}_{\cdot}\rightarrow\mathsf{cMsc}
\]
from the category of simple pointed matroids to \(\mathsf{cMsc}\). This functor induces a fully faithful embedding of projective geometries into commutative mosaics.

Implied scenario detection in the presence of behaviour constraints

Summary: Scenario-based specifications describe how independent components interact to provide system level behaviour. The specified system decomposition and system behaviour can give rise to implied scenarios, which are the result of specifying the global behaviour of a system that will be implemented component-wise. The existence of implied scenarios is an indication that further validation with stakeholders must be done. An implied scenario can be accepted or rejected by stakeholders indicating that the implied scenario is acceptable system behaviour or a situation that should be avoided. In consequence, implied scenarios can be used to iteratively drive requirement elicitation. However, in order to do so, we must be capable of detecting implied scenarios in the presence of rejected implied scenarios, in other words in the presence of behaviour constraints. The contribution of this paper is a technique for detecting implied scenarios in message sequence chart (MSC) specifications that can be used in conjunction with behaviour constraints. The technique is based on building a coordinator component that forces system components to follow the same sequence of basic MSCs as they go through a high-level MSC. The result is a model that behaves as specified in the MSC but does not comply with the MSC architecture. The resulting model is not a proposed implementation, rather a precise model of specified behaviour that can be used in combination with constrained implementation models to detect further implied scenarios.

Formal techniques for analysing scenarios using message sequence charts

Summary: This paper describes light-weight formal techniques based on message sequence charts (MSCs) for capturing and validating early requirements and design. Our focus is on ease of use in specifying, simulating and validating scenarios, and checking their desired properties efficiently. We discuss how the formalism of high level message sequence charts (HMSCs or MSC'96), can be used to capture scenarios in use cases, thus enabling the use of tools for analysing them. We then present two formal semantics for HMSCs -- an intuitive linear time semantics based on runs, and an operational semantics in terms of a labelled transition system. The correctness properties of a collection of MSCs can then be established by efficient algorithms for finding paths in a directed graph representing the precedence relation on the events of the MSCs. We have implemented the operational semantics and the verification algorithms in the form of a simulation and verification tool for analysing scenarios.

Multiple synchrony in MSC

Summary: We propose an extension to Message Sequence Charts (MSC); MSC diagrams comprise processes (called instances) and messages. Messages in MSC are either asynchronous or method calls. Reciprocity obstruction to strong approximation over \(p\)-adic function fields

It is nowadays well-known that arithmetic properties such as the local-global principle, weak approximation and strong approximation for varieties over classical global fields (number fields and function fields of curves over finite fields) admit an obstruction called the \emph{Brauer-Manin} obstruction. Based on the reciprocity result known as the Brauer-Hasse-Noether Theorem, this obstruction was introduced by \textit{Yu. I. Manin} [Actes Congr. Int. Math. 1970, No. 1, 401--411 (1971; Zbl 0239.14010)] for the local-global principle and later extended to other contexts by Colliot-Thélène and Sansuc. This topic in itself has grown so much in the last decades that it earned its own MSC code in the MSC2020 Classification.

A common feature of classical global fields and their completions is that they all have (virtual) cohomological dimension 2. This means that the Brauer group is in some sense the most complicated cohomological invariant of the field and hence one could expect that it might ``explain it all'' concerning the properties above. Lately, there has been a lot of interest in studying these arithmetic properties for fields with higher cohomological dimension. One must replace then the Brauer group and the Brauer-Hasse-Noether Theorem by a higher cohomological invariant and some higher reciprocity law.

The article under review is concerned with the particular case of homogeneous spaces over function fields of \(p\)-adic curves. These are fields of cohomological dimension 3 (and so are their completions). There are several results on this topic already on the literature (see [\textit{D. Harari} et al., J. Algebr. Geom. 25, No. 3, 571--605 (2016; Zbl 1355.14018); Int. Math. Res. Not. 2015, No. 10, 2751--2783 (2015; Zbl 1349.11098); Ann. Inst. Fourier 69, No. 5, 1915--1954 (2019; Zbl 1470.11060)] for tori, [\textit{Y. Tian}, J. Number Theory 220, 128--162 (2021; Zbl 1464.11046); \textit{N. M. Linh}, J. Lond. Math. Soc., II. Ser. 109, No. 1, Article ID e12842, 56 p. (2024; Zbl 1540.14055)] for more general algebraic groups and homogeneous spaces). The author adds to this list by considering strong approximation for homogeneous spaces of certain semisimple simply connected algebraic groups with semisimple stabilizers, which is a case that hadn't been treated before.

Studying (weak or strong) approximation for this type of homogeneous spaces amounts to studying the relation between the set \(H^1(K,G)\) for \(G\) a fixed stabilizer and \(H^1(K_v,G)\) for the different completions \(K_v\) of \(K\). In this sense, the case of classical global fields goes back to the work by Harder and Kneser in the 1960s. Now, the theory of cohomological invariants of algebraic groups teaches us that for fields of low cohomological dimension one should expect a nice behavior since essentially all invariants should be trivial. On the other hand, things should get wilder in higher cohomological dimension. This is how the author manages to find some nice counterexamples to strong approximation in this context, by using the Rost invariant (an invariant of degree 3) and Lichtenbaum duality (a purely \(p\)-adic phenomenon) to define obstructions (see \S3).

For a fixed field \(K\), the Rost invariant takes values in \(H^3(K,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}(2))\), which is precisely the sort of group that replaces the Brauer group in higher reciprocity laws for fields of cohomological dimension 3. This allows the author to explain his counterexamples by means of a reciprocity obstruction in the same vein as those defined in [\textit{J. L. Colliot-Thélène} et al., Trans. Am. Math. Soc. 368, No. 6, 4219--4255 (2016; Zbl 1360.11068); Harari et al., 2015, loc. cit.] (see \S4). Under some technical hypothesis on the arithmetic of the \(p\)-adic curve underlying the field \(K\), the author proves that this obstruction is the only obstruction to strong approximation in the context of these particular homogeneous spaces (Theorem 4.10). He also considers the case of toric stabilizers and gets to a similar result (Theorem 4.11, see also Theorem 5.2, which concerns weak approximation), as well as the case of homogeneous spaces of tori (Corollary 4.17). He thus recovers along the way, under a new light, some results by Harari et al. [2019, loc. cit.] and by Linh in [loc. cit.].

Characteristics and realization of the second generation surface acoustic wave's wavelet device

Summary: To overcome the bulk acoustic wave (BAW), the triple transit signals and the discontinuous frequency band in the first generation surface acoustic wave's (FGSAW's) wavelet device, the full transfer multistrip coupler (MSC) is applied to implement wavelet device, and a novel structure of the second generation surface acoustic wave's (SGSAW's) wavelet device is proposed. The closure of periodic orbits in the Gromov-Hausdorff space

For \(\Delta>0\) a \(\Delta\)-isometry between metric spaces \((X,d_X)\) and \((Y,d_Y)\) is a map \(i: X\to Y\) with the property that \(\max\{d_H(i(X),Y), \sup_{x,x'\in X}\vert d_Y(f(x),f(x'))-d_X(x,x')\vert\}<\Delta,\) where \(d_H\) denotes the usual Hausdorff distance. The \(C^0\) Gromov-Hausdorff distance between maps \(f: X\to X\) and \(g: Y\to Y\) is then defined by \(d_{GH^0}(f,g) = \inf\{\Delta>0\mid \exists{} \Delta\text{-isometries } i: X\to Y, j: Y\to X \text{ such that }d_{C^0}(g\circ i,i\circ f)<\Delta \text{ and }d_{C^0}(j\circ g,f\circ j)<\Delta\}.\) \textit{R. Cubas} [Properties of a stable GH homeomorphism. Uberlândia: Federal University of Uberlândia (MSc Dissertation) (2018)] showed that any continuous transitive map can be \(C^0\) Gromov-Hausdorff approximated by periodic orbits. The converse of this result does not hold in general: For example, the identity on the circle can be \(C^0\) Gromov-Hausdorff approximated by periodic orbits. Here a form of converse is found nonetheless, showing that if the \(C^0\) Gromov-Hausdorff approximating sequence of periodic orbits is converging more quickly than the corresponding periods, then the approximated map is transitive.

Minimum sum coloring of \(P_{4}\)-sparse graphs

Summary: In this paper, we study the minimum sum coloring (MSC) problem on \(P_{4}\)-sparse graphs. First, we introduce the concept of maximal sequence associated with an optimal solution of the MSC problem of any graph. Next, based in such maximal sequences, we show that there is a large sub-family of \(P_{4}\)-sparse graphs for which the MSC problem can be solved in polynomial-time.

Summary: In a recent article, \textit{L. Hella} et al. [in: Proceedings of the 2012 ACM symposium on principles of distributed computing, PODC '12. The mouse set conjecture for sets of reals

The mouse set conjecture, MSC, is the statement: Assume \(\mathrm{AD}^+\). Then for all reals \(x\) and \(y\), the real \(x\) is \(\text{OD}(y)\) (ordinal definable from \(y\)) if and only if there exists a mouse \(\mathcal{M}\) over \(y\) such that \(x\in \mathcal{M}\). The first author proves that MSC holds in the minimal model of \(\text{AD}_{\mathbb{R}}+(\Theta \text{ is regular})\); see [Mem. Am. Math. Soc. 1111, v--vii, 169 p. (2015; Zbl 1403.03110)] where the background material, for the paper under review, is presented. The authors in this paper present conditions under which an analogue conjecture for sets of reals is also true.

In the paper, a hod pair \((\Sigma,\mathcal{P})\) is one that is below \(\text{AD}_{\mathbb{R}}+(\Theta \text{ is regular})\). Given such a pair \((\Sigma,\mathcal{P})\), let
\[
Lp^\Sigma(\mathbb{R})=\cup\{\mathcal{M}: \mathcal{M} \text{ is a sound countably iterable }\Sigma\text{-mouse over }\mathbb{R}\text{ projecting to }\mathbb{R}.\}
\]
The strong mouse set conjecture for sets of reals, SMSC(\(\mathbb{R})\), is the assertion: Assume \(\text{AD}^+\). If \((\Sigma,\mathcal{P})\) is a hod pair such that \(\Sigma\) has branch condensation and is fullness preserving, then for all \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) and \(y\in\mathbb{R}\), the set \(X\) is \(\text{OD}(\Sigma,y)\) if and only if \(X\in Lp^\Sigma(\mathbb{R})\).

Given a hod pair \((\Sigma,\mathcal{P})\), let us say that MSC for \(\Sigma\) holds if for all reals \(x\) and \(y\), the real \(x\) is \(\text{OD}(\Sigma,y)\) if and only if there exists a \(\Sigma\)-mouse \(\mathcal{M}\) over \(y\) such that \(x\in \mathcal{M}\). The main theorem of the paper states that under \(\mathrm{AD}^++V=L(\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}))\) if {\parindent=0.6cm\begin{itemize}\item[--] \(\mathcal{P}\) does not have an inaccessible limit of Woodin cardinals, \item[--] \(\Sigma\) has branch condensation and is fullness preserving, \item[--] MSC for \(\Sigma\) holds, and \item[--] every set of reals \(X\) is \(\text{OD}(\Sigma,y)\) for some real \(y\),

\end{itemize}} then \(\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})=\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})\cap Lp^\Sigma(\mathbb{R})\). As a corollary, the authors conclude that SMSC(\(\mathbb{R})\) holds in the minimal model of \(\text{AD}_{\mathbb{R}}+(\Theta \text{ is regular})\).

Before proving the main theorem, the authors introduce Prikry tree forcing associated with Martin's measure on degrees. This forcing poset is a key tool used to show, under the assumptions, that \(\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})=\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})\cap Lp^\Sigma(\mathbb{R})\).

Numerical estimation of aircrafts' unsteady lateral-directional stability derivatives

A technique for predicting steady and oscillatory aerodynamic loads on general configuration is developed. The prediction is based on the Doublet-Lattice Method, the Slender Body Theory and the Method of Images. Chord and span wise loading on lifting surfaces and longitudinal bodies' load distributions are determined (in horizontal and vertical plane). Configuration may be composed of an assemblage of lifting surfaces (with control surfaces) and bodies (with circular cross sections and a longitudinal variation of radius). Loadings predicted by this method are used to calculate (estimate) steady and unsteady (dynamic) lateral-directional stability derivatives. Short outlines of the used methods are given in the book [\textit{B. Etkin} and \textit{L. Reid}, Dynamics of Flight: Stability and Control, Wiley, (1996)], previous papers of the author as well as in the MSC-NASTRAN handbooks and user guides. Applying the described method, the software DERIV is developed. The obtained results from DERIV are compared to the NASTRAN examples HA21B and HA21D (from the MSC-NASTRAN handbook). In the first example (HA21B), the jet transport wing (BAH wing) is steady rolling, and lateral stability derivatives are determined. In the second example (HA21D), lateral-directional stability derivatives are calculated for a forward-swept-wing (FSW) airplane in antisymmetric quasi-steady maneuvers. Comparing the results from the MSC-NASTRAN handbook and DERIV, an acceptable degree of agreement is achieved.

An eight-node hybrid-stress solid-shell element for geometric nonlinear analysis of elastic shells

Summary: This paper presents eight-node solid-shell elements for geometric nonlinear analysis of elastic shells. To subdue shear, trapezoidal and thickness locking, the assumed natural strain method and an ad hoc modified generalized laminate stiffness matrix are employed. A selectively reduced integrated element is formulated with its membrane and bending shear strain components taken to be constant and equal to the ones evaluated at the element centroid. With the generalized stresses arising from the modified generalized laminate stiffness matrix assumed to be independent from the ones obtained from the displacement, an extended Hellinger--Reissner functional can be derived. By choosing the assumed generalized stresses similar to the assumed stresses of a previous solid element, a hybrid-stress solid-shell element is formulated. Commonly employed geometric nonlinear homogeneous and laminated shell problems are attempted, and our results are close to those of other state-of-the-art elements. Moreover, the hybrid-stress element converges more readily than the selectively reduced integrated element in all benchmark problems.

Estimation of coherence and time delay with ARMA models

Magnitude squared coherence (MSC) and time delay are two important quantities needed for passive detection and localization of a radiating source using several sensors. This paper presents a novel approach to estimating the MSC and time delay from the outputs of two sensors.

It first models the MSC as the product of the transfer functions of two autoregressive moving-average (ARMA) filters. Non-standard inferences in description logics

Description logics (DL) are a family of logic-based knowledge representation (KR) formalisms. They have their root in classical KR formalisms, in frames and semantic networks. The lack of a semantic specification of these formalisms lead to the development of the system KL-ONE equipped with a formal semantics. KL-ONE is considered the fist DL.

The knowledge base of DL-systems consists of two parts -- TBox and ABox. A TBox stores the conceptual (terminological) knowledge of an application domain. In an ABox the assertional knowledge (a world description) is represented.

Concept descriptions are the basic elements of DLs. They are built inductively from concept names (unary predicates), role names (binary predicates), and attribute names using the concept and role constructors. DLs are equipped with a formal logic-based semantics, which is usually defined in a model-theoretic way.

The standard inference services of DLs include computing subconcept/superconcept relationships (subsumption) and checking whether an individual belongs to a concept (instance). Standard inferences are not sufficient when it comes to generating new concept descriptions from given ones, when concepts are specified using different vocabularies or if they are described on different levels of abstraction. The inferences involved are finding the least common subsumer (lcs), finding the most specific concept (msc) and matching of concept description (matching).

At the time when the author's research started, the work concerning non-standard inference problems was at its very beginning. The main goal of the present book is to take non-standard inferences to the level that corresponds to the state of affairs in the investigation of standard inferences. The level can be characterized by the following tasks: to prove formal properties of non-standard inferences, and to provide correct algorithms for solving these inferences together with an analysis of their complexity.

New results concerning the three non-standard inferences -- lcs, msc and matching -- are proven in the book. An in-depth analysis as well as provably sound and complete algorithms for lcs, msc and matching (for the description logics \({\mathcal A}{\mathcal L}{\mathcal N}{\mathcal S}\), \({\mathcal A}{\mathcal L}{\mathcal N}^*\), and \({\mathcal A}{\mathcal L}{\mathcal E}\) and for some of their sublanguages) are provided in the book.

The ''constant'' bending moment three-noded triangle

Summary: This paper addresses the problem of constructing an ideal three-noded flat triangular plate bending finite element model with constant approximations to bending moments. Such a simple element is potentially advantageous in the nonlinear analysis of thin-walled shells, but there are fundamental difficulties associated with achieving an element stiffness matrix whose rank is sufficient to avoid the occurrence of spurious mechanisms. An innovative solution is explored which yields a properly constituted stiffness matrix of correct rank by introducing the unusual, yet practical expedient of `virtually constant' bending moments. Numerical results for benchmark plate bending problems where a direct energy comparison is available show barely perceptible differences to those obtained using the conventional six-noded constant bending moment triangle.

The maximum squared correlation, sum capacity, and total asymptotic efficiency of minimum total-squared-correlation binary signature sets

Tensors and Riemannian geometry. With applications to differential equations

This book presents basic geometric and group theoretical methods in partial differential equations and indicates their fruitful applications to the theory of relativity. As the author informs in the preface, it is based on series of lectures he has delivered in various universities.

The book is divided into three parts. Part I, entitled ``Tensors and Riemannian spaces'', consists of four chapters. The basic notions of differential and Riemannian geometry are introduced in Chapter 3. Chapter 4 addresses the basics of the group theoretical background. Here, notions such as isometric motion, conformal motion, invariant, Killing equation, generalized Killing equation (for conformal motions) are described. Chapter 2, entitled ``Conservation laws'', though thematically different from the rest of Part I, is crucial for what follows. Here, fundamentals of theoretical physics are laid. After the derivation of Kepler's laws out of certain conserved quantities the author discusses conservation laws of general systems of differential equations in detail. In the case of Euler-Lagrange equations, for every infinitesimal generator of transformations that leave the variational integral invariant, Noether's theorem renders a conserved vector explicitly. More generally, in the case of so-called nonlinearly self-adjoint systems, for every infinitesimal symmetry of the system a conserved vector can be likewise obtained by the use of the so-called formal Lagrangian. Unfortunately, the author does not indicate any procedure of determining infinitesimal symmetries, although this issue is of practical importance.

Part II bears the title ``Riemannian spaces of second-order equations'' and consists of Chapters 5--7. The author starts by writing a general second-order linear differential equation in covariant form (Chapter 5). In Chapter 6, he passes to a system of covariant equations, which is supposed to determine the infinitesimal symmetries of the given differential equation. Again, the author does not explain this crucial step, but refers the reader to the literature [\textit{L. V. Ovsyannikov}, Group Properties of Differential Equations (Siberian Branch, USSR Academy of Sciences, Novosibirsk) (1962)]. In the sequel, he focuses on four-dimensional pseudo-Riemannian spaces of signature \((---+)\) and gives criteria for their conformal groups to be nontrivial (i.e., wider than the isometric group) or for the spaces to be conformally flat (i.e., conformal to the Minkowski space). In this context, examples of conformally invariant second-order linear differential equations are discussed. Chapter 7 considers four-dimensional spaces with nontrivial conformal groups. After the Cauchy problem for the wave equation has been solved with the help of Fourier transforms, geodesics are explicitly computed, and the Huygens principle is discussed.

Part III, entitled ``Theory of relativity'', can be viewed as an application of the aforementioned mathematical notions and methods to the theory of relativity. It consists of Chapters 8 and 9. We cite the author from its introduction: ``Chapter 8 is a brief introduction to the mathematical background of the special relativity. The derivation of the conservation laws in relativistic mechanics is based on the Lie group approach rather than on physical considerations. Two fundamental relativistic (i.e., Lorentz invariant) equations of theoretical physics, the Maxwell and Dirac equations, are discussed from the group point of view. A possibility offered by groups of generalized motions for constructing particular solutions to the Einstein equations in the theory of general relativity is also discussed in Chapter 8.''

Chapter 9 addresses the so-called de Sitter space, which is a curved four-dimensional pseudo-Riemannian space of signature \((+---)\). The isometric motions of this space constitute the so-called de Sitter group. To study this group, the author applies a theory of so-called approximate transformation groups, described in detail in [the author, Selected works. Volume III: Doctor of Science thesis, approximate symmetries, Lie groups in mathematical modelling. ALGA Publications. Karlskrona: ALGA, Blekinge Institute of Technology (2008; Zbl 1314.01037)] (Paper 2). For this purpose, the de Sitter group is regarded as a perturbation of the Poincaré group (i.e., the group of isometries of the Minkowski space) by a (small) constant curvature. As the author states in the introduction, the presentation of Chapter 9 is based on [the author, Selected works. Volume II: MSc and PhD theses, nonlocal symmetries, approximate symmetries, preliminary group classification, Lie group analysis -- a microscope of mathematical modelling. ALGA Publications. Karlskrona: ALGA, Blekinge Institute of Technology (2006; Zbl 1307.01021), pp. 244--280] .

This book introduces classical notions and methods in an unusual way, primarily in its first two parts. It avoids abstract conceptual bodies and follows a computational, coordinate-based approach, which reflects the historical development of the ideas. The frequent historical and philosophical citations, especially in Part III, promote the understanding. A reader who is less familiar with physics might expect more introductory information on certain subjects as, for instance, the Huygens principle or the Dirac equation. From the viewpoint of typing, the book is not free of misprints.

To sum up, this book offers a good introduction into the interplay of differential geometry, Lie theory, differential equations, and relativity, and stimulates further reading and research on these fields.

Log-linear models and logistic regression

[For reviews of the first and second editions from 1990 and 2007, see [Zbl 0711.62050] and [Zbl 0880.62073].]

Like its predecessors, this book focuses on log-linear models and logistic regression for categorical data. The third edition consists of 15 chapters. Various combinations of chapters can be used as a textbook: Fundamentals accessible to undergraduates in statistics, data science, and mathematics are covered in Chapters~1--4. Chapters~5--9 present intermediate material aimed at MSc students in statistics. For advanced MSc or Ph.D. students, Chapters~10, 11, 12, and 15 could be incorporated into a course. Chapters~13 and 14 read more like parts of a research monograph than standard course material, as they are less self-contained. A few other chapters include brief detours that may not fit well in a course. However, for most of the book, only prior knowledge of regression, analysis of variance, and basic probability and statistical hypothesis testing is required, with some familiarity with linear model theory being useful.

Chapter~1, \textit{Introduction}, reviews fundamental concepts such as conditional independence, random variables, and expected values. It also discusses distributions commonly used in contingency table analysis -- including the binomial, multinomial, product multinomial, and Poisson -- while also addressing overdispersion.

Chapter~2, \textit{Two-Dimensional Tables and Simple Logistic Regression}, provides an elementary treatment of these topics, including the odds ratio. Chapter~3, \textit{Three-Dimensional Tables}, examines independence and odds ratio models for three-dimensional tables under multinomial sampling, along with the iterative proportional fitting algorithm for estimating expected cell counts. It also introduces log-linear models for higher-dimensional tables (three or more) and model selection criteria. Additionally, Chapter~3 presents shorthand notation of the form [1][2][3] or [12][3] for representing (conditional) independence of factors.

Chapter~4, \textit{Logistic Regression, Logit Models, and Logistic Discrimination}, covers regression models for binary responses, model fit assessment, logistic regression diagnostics, and variable selection. It also discusses analysis of variance-type models and concludes with the concepts of discrimination and allocation in logistic regression.

Chapter~5, \textit{Independence Relationships and Graphical Models}, considers models for four- and higher-dimensional tables, graphical representations, and conditions under which tables can be collapsed. Graphical models are not central to this chapter or the rest of the book; rather, the focus is on comparing them with other models for contingency tables. Chapter~6, \textit{Model Selection Methods and Model Evaluation}, discusses strategies for model selection in high-dimensional settings, emphasizing stepwise methods and the selection criteria introduced in Chapter~3.

Chapter~7, \textit{Models for Factors with Quantitative Levels}, explores models incorporating quantitative factor levels, stressing that their validity depends on the appropriateness of the assigned scores. These models use log-linear formulations of expected cell counts. Chapter~8, \textit{Fixed and Random Zeros}, addresses contingency tables with zero cell counts.

Chapter~9, \textit{Generalized Linear Models}, covers core topics such as distribution families, model fitting, and dispersion estimation. Chapter~10, \textit{The Matrix Approach to Log-Linear Models}, summarizes key results in maximum likelihood theory for log-linear models using matrix notation, including Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares. Chapter~11, \textit{The Matrix Approach to Logistic Models}, extends this framework to logistic regression and logit models, highlighting their equivalence with log-linear models, and presents selection criteria, likelihood equations, and the Newton-Raphson procedure.

Chapter~12, \textit{Maximum Likelihood Theory for Log-Linear Models}, discusses the theoretical foundations of fitting log-linear models via maximum likelihood, including finite-sample and asymptotic properties. Chapter~13, \textit{Bayesian Binomial Regression}, first covers prior specification, then inference for regression coefficients and \(LD_\alpha\), and concludes with diagnostics via various influence functions.

This edition adds two new chapters. Chapter~14, \textit{Exact Conditional Tests}, explains the two- and three-factor cases as well as the general theory; compared to other chapters, it is relatively terse. Chapter~15, \textit{Correspondence Analysis}, reviews Singular Value Decomposition and details the calculations underlying graphical methods.

Overall, this is a solid work that serves primarily as a textbook but also as a valuable reference for the analysis of categorical data using log-linear models and logistic regression.

Closed classes of Boolean functions.

Tihs book presents several Russian contributions to the study of Post classes of Boolean functions. Recall that this term designates those classes of truth functions that are closed with respect to superpositions.

A new approach to the determination of the partially ordered set (with respect to inclusion) of all these classes is provided in Chapter 1, and for each class a finite basis is displayed.

Chapter 2 studies classes of predicates over \(\{0,1\}\), closed with respect to \(\&\), \(\exists x_i\) and replacement of variables. A (Boolean) function \(f\) of \(n\) variables is said to preserve a (Boolean) predicate \(\rho\) of \(k\) variables provided
\[
\rho(x_{11},\dots, x_{k1})\& \cdots \& \rho(x_{1n},\dots, x_{kn})\Rightarrow \rho(f(x_{11},\dots, x_{1n}),\dots, f(x_{k1},\dots, x_{kn})).
\]
For every set \(R\) of predicates, \(\text{Pol}(R)\) denotes the set of those functions which preserve \(\rho\) for all \(\rho\in R\). For every set \(F\) of functions, \(\text{Inv}(F)\) denotes the set of those predicates which are preserved by all \(f\in F\). Then Inv and Pol establish a contravariant Galois connection between the powerset of the set of all Boolean functions and the powerset of the set of all Boolean predicates. The Galois-closed classes \(F= \text{Pol}(\text{Inv}(F))\) are exactly those closed classes \(F\) which contain all the projections, that is, all closed classes except the three minimal classes of the poset of closed classes. The Galois-closed classes \(R= \text{Inv}(\text{Pol}(R))\) are exactly those closed classes \(R\) which contain all the diagonals (the diagonal of an equivalence relation \(\varepsilon\) on the set \(\{1,\dots,k\}\) is the predicate \(i\varepsilon j\Rightarrow x_i= x_j\)). The chapter also provides a characterization of those closed classes which can be written in the form \(\text{Pol}(R)\) where \(R\) is a finite set of predicates, as well as an explicit list of them.

Chapter 3 extends the previous theory to classes of function vectors \((f_1,\dots, f_m)\). Chapter 4 introduces three new closures for classes of Boolean functions, called parametric closure, positive closure and \(S\)-closure. There are 25 parametric-closed classes and a characterization of parametric completeness is provided. There are 6 positive-closed classes and 15 \(S\)-closed classes.

Reviewer's remarks: 1) In order to define the closed classes under investigation, the author unncessarily passes through formal expressions which are carelessly defined. 2) The terms ``Galois theory'' and ``Post algebra'' are used in a sense which is not the conventional one: the latter correspond to the MSC Classification sections 12F10 and 03G20, respectively.

Spectral flow. A functional analytic and index-theoretic approach

This quite interesting book, consisting of twelve chapters and one appendix, thoroughly handles spectral flows in their diverse aspects and applications. The authors present this deep subject in a form that is palatable for MSc. students possessing basic Functional Analysis knowledge, introducing them to topics and particular results obtained by recent research. Some familiarity with \textit{T. Kato} [Perturbation theory for linear operators. Reprint of the corr. print. of the 2nd ed. 1980. Berlin: Springer-Verlag (1995; Zbl 0836.47009)], and fair accessibility to the fundamental books by \textit{I. Gohberg} et al. [Classes of linear operators. Vol. I. Basel etc.: Birkhäuser Verlag (1990; Zbl 0745.47002); Classes of linear operators. Vol. II. Basel: Birkhäuser Verlag (1993; Zbl 0789.47001)], will be quite helpful to the reader, as well as, an open mind relative to the occasional use of Dirac bracket notation. The text makes short incursions into other areas of Mathematics, beyond Functional Analysis, among them symplectic geometry, topology, including K-theory. The student must be willing to consult the corresponding literature, whenever needed. The book itself begins with the finite-dimensional case, whereby different approaches to the spectral flow concept are presented, depending on the classes of matrices one is considering. The article by \textit{J. Phillips} [Can. Math. Bull. 39, No. 4, 460--467 (1996; Zbl 0878.19001)] plays a fundamental role in authors motivation for adopting a proper, for their purpose, spectral flow definition. The preparation for the Bott-Maslov index introduction, via the spectral flow, and its relation with the Conley-Zehnder index, is done first in the finite-dimensional context (Chapter 2) the general case being postponed for later (Chapter 9). After a brief presentation of compact and bounded Fredholm operators on infinite dimensional Hilbert spaces (Chapter 3) the index concept for bounded Fredholm operators, and some of its properties, are introduced. The nice Calderon-Fedosov formula (Theorem 3.3.7) and the Weil criterion for essential spectrum (Proposition 3.4.7) are also detached. The topological interrelations with the Fredholm operators index, through spectral flow, are then presented (Sections 3.5--3.7). Chapter four introduces part of the book backbone since it brings the spectral flow concept of a continuous path of bounded self-adjoint Fredholm operators, some of its basic properties, and extensions to certain classes of unitary, including essentially gapped, operators. The methods in the chapter are extended in subsequent chapters to more general contexts. One should stress that the authors spectral flow concept (Definition 4.1.2), adapted from Phillips definition, allows half integers as possible values, with its formula naturally generalizing the finite-dimensional context, while in Phillips approach it assumes only integer values. Kato pairs, introduced in his book, quoted previously, motivate the authors to handle Fredholm pairs of projections in chapter 5, for which indices are introduced, and several properties and characterizations for different types of projections are given ( see Sections 5.2--5.5). In the sequel explicit formulas for the spectral flow, through the index, for different types of paths and pairs are obtained. Inspired by the paper of \textit{P. M. Fitzpatrick} et al. [J. Funct. Anal. 162, No. 1, 52--95 (1999; Zbl 0915.58091)], the authors give, through the Morse index, an alternative formulation to the spectral flow (see Theorem 5.9.6). The case of unbounded Fredholm operators is handled in the sixth chapter, after a review of different sorts of topologies ( induced by gap and Riesz metrics ) on the set of closed operators, followed by a summary of their basic properties. A new short proof of a Cordes and Labrousse theorem, see [\textit{H. O. Cordes} and \textit{J. P. Labrousse}, J. Math. Mech. 12, 693--719 (1963; Zbl 0148.12402)], is also included. The authors sum up detailed expositions, such as [\textit{D. E. Edmunds} and \textit{W. D. Evans}, Spectral theory and differential operators. Oxford: Oxford University Press (1987; Zbl 0628.47017)]. They conclude the sixth chapter with unbounded self-adjoint Fredholm operators with properties involving the gap and Riesz topologies related to homotopy theory. In particular, the important case of operators with compact resolvent for which the connection with A. Connes' non-commutative geometry is pointed out (see Theorem 6.4.2 and its proof).

One of the highlights of the book is chapter seven, where the spectral flow for gap continuous paths of unbounded self-adjoint Fredholm operators is handled in the spirit of the article by \textit{B. Booss-Bavnbek} et al. [Can. J. Math. 57, No. 2, 225--250 (2005; Zbl 1085.58018)]. The Atiyah, Patodi, and Singer eta-invariant is then related to the spectral flow of a suitable path of self-adjoint Fredholm operators (see Theorem 7.2.2) as first done by \textit{E. Getzler} [Topology 32, No. 3, 489--507 (1993; Zbl 0801.46088)] and later by \textit{M. C. Georgescu} [Spectral flow in semi-finite von Neumann algebras. University Victoria (PhD thesis) (2013)]. The authors present a new method of proof of this beautiful result partially based on previous work by \textit{A. Carey} and \textit{J. Phillips} [Can. J. Math. 50, No. 4, 673--718 (1998; Zbl 0915.46063); \(K\)-Theory 31, No. 2, 135--194 (2004; Zbl 1051.19004)]. In the case of paths of self-adjoint Fredholm operators with compact resolvent, originating from families of Hamiltonian systems, as in [\textit{J. Robbin} and \textit{D. Salamon}, Bull. Lond. Math. Soc. 27, No. 1, 1--33 (1995; Zbl 0859.58025)], the spectral flow relates to the Conley-Zehnder index (see Propositions 7.3.1 and 7.3.3). The chapter concludes with a characterization of the spectral flow through the Fredholm index, extending a previous result (Theorem 3.5.1) that holds for any continuous path of self-adjoint matrices with invertible limits, here though the generalization to infinite dimension is constrained to some types of paths (see Theorem 7.4.1), a new proof for this result is provided, compare with the paper by Robbin and Salamon quoted above.

The eighth chapter follows the model of the excellent book by B. Booß-Bavnbek and K. P. Wojciechowski, in particular Part II. It handles homotopy groups of sets of Fredholm operators, as well Fredholm pairs, through it, several topological properties of these specific sets are proved, as well as a further spectral flow characterization as an application of the previous beautiful results (see Theorems 8.2.2, 8.3.1, 8.4.1 and their corollaries). The chapter concludes with the homotopy groups of Fredholm pairs (see Theorem 8.5.4) and of unbounded self-adjoint Fredholm operators ( see theorems 8.6.1 - 8.6.3 ), these later results follow the treatment by \textit{M. Prokhorova} [``Spaces of unbounded Fredholm operators. I. Homotopy equivalences'', Preprint, \url{arXiv:2110.14359}]. The theory of the Bott-Maslov and Conley-Zehnder indices previously presented are extended in the ninth chapter to infinite-dimensional Krein spaces, for an introduction of the latter spaces, see e.g. [\textit{T. Ya. Azizov} and \textit{I. S. Iokhvidov}, Linear operators in space with an indefinite metric. Transl. from the Russian by E. R. Dawson. Chichester: John Wiley \&| Sons Ltd. (1989; Zbl 0714.47028)].

The ninth chapter includes, beyond the characterization of maximally isotropic spaces in terms of Krein signature (see Proposition 9.2.9) and the indices extensions quoted above, also, as an application, a study of oscillation theory for bound states of scattering systems, see Section 9.7, in particular Theorem 9.7.4.

The tenth chapter introduces unbounded Fredholm modules, also called spectral triples, see [\textit{A. Connes}, Noncommutative geometry. Transl. from the French by Sterling Berberian. San Diego, CA: Academic Press (1994; Zbl 0818.46076)] and relates them with index pairings. A fundamental result due to Connes (see Theorem 10.1.4) and the theta-summable Dirac operator notion of a Fredholm module are introduced with spectral flow formulas ( see Theorems 10.2.1 and 10.2.3). The following two sections deal with even, respectively odd, unbounded Fredholm modules, through a finite-dimensional self-adjoint matrix, called spectral localizer, see Theorems 10.3.1 and 10.4.1, as the articles by \textit{T. A. Loring} and \textit{H. Schulz-Baldes} [Can. Math. Bull. 62, No. 2, 373--381 (2019; Zbl 1410.19002); J. Noncommut. Geom. 14, No. 1, 1--23 (2020; Zbl 1441.19011)]. The last section of the chapter introduces a new link between the spectral flow and the eta-invariant, to this aim a dimension concept for the Dirac operator of a Fredholm module is needed (Definition 10.5.1). This beautiful chapter concludes with Theorem 10.5.9 and Proposition 10.5.10 on the previously mentioned link, see by [\textit{T. A. Loring} and \textit{H. Schulz-Baldes}, New York J. Math. 23, 1111--1140 (2017; Zbl 1384.46048)].

The eleventh chapter handles the spectral flow in semi-finite von Neumann algebras. Some basic elements, and facts, on von Neumann algebras are recalled initially and a generalization of Atkinson's theorem (11.1.6). The section on the sequel introduces the so-called skew-corner Fredholm operators, see Theorem 11.2.3 and the article by \textit{A. L. Carey} et al. [Adv. Math. 202, No. 2, 517--554 (2006; Zbl 1101.46045)]. In the third section, the authors introduce the semi-finite Fredholm pair concept and present several of its properties, besides a characterization (see Theorem 11.3.7). Further, the notion of semi-finite spectral flow is introduced altogether with some properties. The chapter concludes by presenting formulas on the relations between the semi-finite index and the semi-finite spectral flow (see Theorem 11.5.1 and Propositions 11.5.4) and an application thereof.

The twelfth, and, last chapter has the purpose of presenting applications of spectral flow, in variational bifurcation theory. One proves the existence of a bifurcation of critical points, Theorem 12.2.1, first proved in the paper of Fitzpatrick, Pejsachowicz, and Recht quoted above. The chapter concludes with further application to Hamiltonian systems (see Theorems 12.3.3--12.3.5). The main text concludes with a short appendix containing a sum up of some technical results.

The book represents a well-researched solid reference on a rich subject, that encompasses an important vast territory. It is hard reading for beginning MSc. degree students, the reward though is well worth the corresponding effort.

New foundations in mathematics. The geometric concept of number

As one can see in the MSC classification given to this book, it covers a wide range of subjects in mathematics. It is conceived as a textbook. Each chapter is divided in small sections making it easier for a student to follow each topic. At the end of each section a list of exercises is given. Within the text, the author included many references to links in the internet, some in Wikipedia but others in sites from researchers working on the subject, with very interesting data on the subject as well as further reading. A good example is the end of Chapter 3 (Geometric algebra) where the link gives the reader the possibility to know more on Clifford algebras. I linked to some of these sites and could check how relevant the material could be to the topic it is related to. The book also includes some detailed instructions on the plotting of some surfaces or graphs with Mathematica. Considering all the mathematical topics introduced in this book it is not a very thick book (351 pages), but it is self-contained.

The book is divided into 18 chapters. Most of these chapters introduce basic mathematical concepts in some specific undergraduate or graduate courses but it is not usual to see all of them in the same textbook, if the book does not aim to be an encyclopedia. The first chapter introduces modular numbers and polynomials and calculates the Lagrange-Sylvester interpolation polynomial of any function. This chapter includes a special section dedicated to the generalized Taylor's theorem. In the second chapter the author introduces complex and hyperbolic numbers, including, in a section on the hyperbolic polar form, detailed explanations on the \(\rho\)-hyperbola, hyperbolic angles and the computation of the hyperbolic arc length along the hyperbola \(x^2-y^2=1\). There are also sections on inner and outer products and hyperbolic rotations. The last section of this chapter explains the relation of hyperbolic numbers to special relativity and Lorentzian geometry. The third chapter introduces geometric algebra with the usual sections on geometric algebra of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), vector derivative in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), orthogonal transformations. Chapters 4--9 give definitions and properties on vector spaces and matrices, outer products and determinants, systems of linear equations, linear transformations and linear and bilinear forms. In Chapter 10 (Hermitian inner product spaces) the author introduces the unitary geometric algebra \(U_{p,q}=U(\mathbb{H}^{p,q})\) of the Hermitian space \(\mathbb{H}^{p,q}\). This chapter includes the orthogonality relationships in pseudo-Euclidean spaces, the unitary geometric algebra of pseudo-Euclidean spaces, Hermitian orthogonality, Hermitian, normal and unitary operators and a special section on principal correlation and polar and singular value decomposition.

In Chapter 11 (Geometry of moving planes), the author explains how the concept of 2-dimensional space-time in the geometric algebra \(\mathbb{G}_1\) (Chapter 2) generalizes to the 4-dimensional space-time of special relativity in the geometric algebra \(\mathbb{G}_3\). The chapter includes sections on relative orthonormal basis, relative geometric algebras and moving planes. In this last section the author considers various concepts in special relativity such as the Lorentz boost and the addition of velocities. There is a special section (Splitting the plane) where it is explained how the geometric algebra \(\mathbb{G}_2\) of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is split into the geometric algebra \(\mathbb{G}_{1,2}\) of Minkowski space-time \(\mathbb{R}^{1,2}\). Chapter 12 deals with the representation of the symmetric group with sections on twisted product, geometric numbers in \(\mathbb{G}_{n,m}\), the twisted product of geometric numbers and symmetric groups in geometric algebras. The chapter includes a special section (The heart of the matter) that explains the formalization of the regular representations of the symmetric groups that were found in the previous section.

Chapters 13--15 explain basic differential geometry of curves surfaces including calculus on surfaces. Chapter 16 deals with different types of mappings between surfaces: projective, conformal, Möbius. This chapter includes a special section on affine connections. Chapter 17 deals with non-Euclidean and projective geometries, and Chapter 18 with Lie algebras and Lie groups.
