Coin-turning, random walks and inhomogeneous Markov chains

The authors have chosen an appropriate title well corresponding to the content of the book. In fact, this is a modern monograph on inhomogeneous Markov chains. Interesting stochastic models are treated and good questions are asked, followed by answers and proofs. It is a pleasure to read the book and get a satisfaction by the smooth and elegant way of passing from one concept or model to another one. The authors of this book have published a series of original papers in top journals, so their contribution is new, fresh and essential. Moreover, other scientists followed and further studied some of the models. It is great to see most recent developments in this area carefully collected and well presented now in a monograph form.

The book follows more or less established good traditions. In Chapter 1 we find notions such as Lévy's Borel-Cantelli lemma, anti-concentration inequalities of Kolmogorov, Rogozin and Kesten, basics of martingales, moment problems and point processes and measures. Chapter 2 deals with time-homogeneous Markov chains: Chapman-Kolmogorov equations, transience and recurrence properties, reversibility, total variation convergence. Chapter 4 explains some difficulties arising when we study inhomogeneous Markov chains. Thus we arrive at two of the main chapters, 4 and 5, entirely devoted to ``Coin Turning''. The authors tell first intuitively, then strictly, what does this term mean: it is a time-inhomogeneous Markov chain with just two states, \(\mathsf{S} = \{T, H\}\), or \(\mathsf{S} = \{0, 1\}.\) The idea is to follow an action called ``turn over''. It only looks that this model is elementary, however, there is a list of questions to ask which need serious efforts to find the answers. A lot of stuff from discrete probability is involved and special functions from analysis are needed. Several beautiful results are presented with their detailed proofs. One can see the difference when studying the three cases, critical, supercritical and subcritical. It is shown that the coin-turn random walk obeys interesting properties while the scaled random quantities satisfy the WLLN. Urn models and related time-inhomogeneous Markov processes are treated in Chapter 7. Moreover, the urns' specifics are combined with the coin-turning. Rademacher random walks are considered in Chapter 8. More advanced material, e.g., coin-turning random walks in higher dimensions, is included in the last two chapters, 9 and 10. The authors study a class of conservative random walks and urn-related random walks with specific drift. Recurrence, transience, and multidimensional scaling limits are studied.

There are useful graphical illustrations to some concepts and results. At the end of each chapter there are exercises with short hints and, in a couple of cases, historical notes. The bibliography looks exhaustive as is also the subject index.

In brief, this monograph is a great addition to the collection of fundamental sources in modern theory of stochastic processes. Any scientist in this area would find novelties eventually inspiring further studies. The book can be used as a source for a special advanced course addressed to university MSc and PhD students.

It can be predicted that the monograph will be well met by the community of probability theory. Many individuals may find deserving to have own copies, however, the monograph must be available in any mathematics library.

Estimation of coherence and time delay with ARMA models

Magnitude squared coherence (MSC) and time delay are two important quantities needed for passive detection and localization of a radiating source using several sensors. This paper presents a novel approach to estimating the MSC and time delay from the outputs of two sensors.

It first models the MSC as the product of the transfer functions of two autoregressive moving-average (ARMA) filters. The ARMA coefficients are then determined by a least squares, matrix pseudoinverse solution to the estimation equation. Time delay estimation follows as a byproduct, since both phase and MSC estimates are now available.

Remarks on finding critical points

Let \(F\) be a real \(C^ 1\) function defined on a Banach space \(X\). In the first part of the paper there are presented some applications of Ekeland's Principle in obtaining critical points of functions \(F\) which satisfy the Palais-Smale property. The main result is given by Theorem 1, proved in this part by using Ekeland's Principle. In the second part is presented a general deformation theorem (Theorem 3). Next a new proof of a recent theorem of Ghoussoub (Theorem 2) is given by using deformation Theorem 3. In the third part, the authors apply Theorem 2 to functions \(F\) which are bounded below and satisfy the Palais-Smale property. Finally, in the Appendix, the authors give a new proof of Theorem 1 based on deformation Theorem 3.

Number theory: an introduction to mathematics. Part B

This part starts with an introduction into the theory of quadratic spaces, culminating with the proof of the Hasse-Minkowski theorem. The main results of the geometry of numbers follow, with Minkowski's convex body theorem and Mahler's compactness theorem. The chapter on prime numbers contains Chebyshev's inequalities, the Prime Number Theorem (proved via Ikehara's theorem) and a discussion of Riemann's Hypothesis. The proof of Dirichlet's theorem on primes in progression follows, and then linear representations of finite groups are introduced and their main properties established. A chapter on uniform distribution and ergodic theory follows, containing Weyl's criterion, Birkhoff's ergodic theorem and Poincaré's recurrence theorem. As an application van der Waerden's theorem on partitions of the set of integers is proved. The penultimate chapter brings an introduction to elliptic functions and the book is concluded with several arithmetical results: we find there Jacobi's four squares theorem, Rogers-Ramanujan identities and elliptic curves with a proof of the theorem of Mordell.

As in part A (see Zbl 0997.11001 above) each chapter brings also broad comments and references to further reading. The book is a welcome addition to the literature.

Actions of Polish groups and classification problems

The paper comprises the general Glimm-Effros dichotomy; actions of Polish groups, countable groups, locally compact groups and infinite symmetric groups; Hjorth's theory of turbulence. The paper contains the following results: the general Glimm-Effros dichotomy theorem, the Becker-Kechris theorem, the Feldman-Moore theorem, the Slaman-Steel theorem, the Dougherty-Jackson-Kechris theorem, the Ornstein-Weiss theorem, the Kechris-Sofronidis theorem.

Nonconvex minimization theorems and fixed point theorems in complete metric spaces

Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. The authors first introduce the concept of \(w\)-distance, it is a generalization of metric \(d\) on \(X\). They establish some properties of \(w\)-distance and prove a nonconvex minimization theorem which improves a result of Takahashi. They also improve Caristi's fixed point theorem and Ekeland's \(E\)-variational principle. They also prove a fixed point theorem in a complete metric space and apply this theorem to prove Subrahmanyam's fixed point theorem, Kaman's fixed point theorem, and Čirič's fixed point theorem. The results of this paper seem useful, interesting, and original.

A rough set view on Bayes' theorem

Summary: Rough set theory offers a new perspective on Bayes' theorem. The look on Bayes' theorem offered by rough set theory reveals that any data set (decision table) satisfies the total probability theorem and Bayes' theorem. These properties can be used directly to draw conclusions from objective data without referring to subjective prior knowledge and its revision if new evidence is available. Thus, the rough set view on Bayes' theorem is rather objective in contrast to subjective classical interpretation of the theorem.

A fixed-point approach to stable matchings and some applications.

Summary: We describe a fixed-point based approach to the theory of bipartite stable matchings. By this, we provide a common framework that links together seemingly distant results, like the stable marriage theorem of Gale and Shapley, the Mendelsohn-Dulmage theorem, the Kundu-Lawler theorem, Tarski's fixed-point theorem, the Cantor-Bernstein theorem, Pym's linking theorem, or the monochromatic path theorem of Sands et al. In this framework, we formulate a matroidgeneralization of the stable marriage theorem and study the lattice structure of generalized stable matchings. Based on the theory of lattice polyhedra and blocking polyhedra, we extend results of Vande Vate and Rothblum on the bipartite stable matching polytope.

The implicit function theorem. History, theory, and applications

This book is devoted to basic results with the generally accepted name Implicit Function Theorem (sometimes Inverse Function Theorem) and which appear everywhere, beginning with elementary courses of Calculus and ending up with fundamental monographs on Functional Analysis, Differential and Integral Equations, Calculus of Variations, and so on.

The book consists of 6 chapters. Chapter 1 ``Introduction to the Implicit Function Theorem'' presents an informal version of the Implicit Function Theorem and its Paradigm. Chapter 2 ``History'' describes the basic steps on the way from heuristic thinking on implicit functions to up-to-date formulations of the Implicit Function Theorem (Newton, Lagrange, Cauchy). Chapter 3 ``Basic Ideas'' deals with the classical Implicit Function Theorem and gives its different proofs: inductive, classical (on the base of construction leading to the theorem about conditions for local homeomorphism), and Goursat's (on the base of successive approximations or Banach-Caccioppoli fixed point principle); in this chapter one can find also the classical Rank Theorem and Decomposition Theorem. Chapter 4 ``Applications'' is devoted to standard applications of the Implicit Function Theorem to ordinary differential equations, the theory of surfaces and others. Chapter 5 ``Variations and Generalizations'' presents the Weierstrass Preparation Theorem, a variant of the Implicit Function Theorem without Differentiability, an Inverse Function Theorem for Continuous Mapping, and some singular cases of the Implicit Function Theorem. The last chapter ``Advanced Implicit Function Theorem'' deals with the Analytic Implicit Function Theorem, Hadamard's Global Implicit Function Theorem, the Implicit Function Theorem via the Newton-Kantorovich Method, and the Nash-Moser Implicit Function Theorem.

It seems that the book is concerned with all problems related to implicit function theorems. However, this book really does not cover all fields with the name ``Implicit Function Theorem''. So, the authors do not recall G. Peano, E. Goursat, G. A. Bliss, Young, A. Lamson, S. M. Lozinskii, and others, who made a significant contribution in this field; the authors do not consider different variants of the Implicit Function Theorem in Banach spaces for operators differentiable only in separate points, or variants of the Implicit Function Theorem based on fixed point principles different from Banach-Caccioppoli; the authors also omitted variants of the Implicit Function Theorem for operators in locally convex spaces or for operators in spaces of formal power series. One can find some information in this direction in [\textit{J. Appell}, \textit{A. Vignoli} and \textit{P. P. Zabreiko}, Expo. Math. 14, No. 5, 385-424 (1996; Zbl 0869.26003)].

However, in general, this book is the first that is especially devoted to the Implicit Function Theorem. The authors offer a useful and fascinating manuscript which should be of interest and useful to graduate and postgraduate students, professional mathematicians, teachers as well as researchers. Most of them will be able to find all fundamental ideas in the field and simple and transparent proofs of all main implicit function theorems and theorems closely related to these.

Complex function theory

This is an introductory course in the theory of functions of one complex variable. The material and its presentation are rather classical. The stress is put on precision and details of the formulated results.

The contents cover the following topics:

I. Complex Numbers.

II. Complex differentiation: polynomials and rational functions, Cauchy-Riemann equations, holomorphic functions, conformality, harmonic functions.

III. Linear-fractional transformations.

IV. Elementary functions: \(e^z\), hyperbolic functions, trigonometric functions, logarithms, branches of \(\arg z\) and \(\log z\), inverses of holomorphic functions, inverse trigonometric functions, powers, analytic continuation and Riemann surfaces.

V. Power series: Cauchy-Hadamard theorem, differentiation of power series, Cauchy product, division of power series.

VI. Complex integration.

VII. Core versions of Cauchy's theorem, and consequences: Cauchy's theorem for a triangle, Cauchy's theorem for a convex region, existence of a primitive, Cauchy's formula for a circle, mean value property, Cauchy integrals, Cauchy product, converse of Goursat's lemma, Liouville theorem, fundamental theorem of algebra, zeros of holomorphic functions, the identity theorem, Weierstrass convergence theorem, maximum modulus principle, Schwarz's lemma, existence of harmonic conjugates, mean value property for harmonic functions, identity theorem for harmonic functions, maximum principle for harmonic functions, harmonic functions in higher dimensions.

VIII. Laurent series and isolated singularities: Laurent series, Cauchy's formula for an annulus, existence of Laurent series representations, isolated singularities, criterion for a removable singularity, criterion for a pole, Casorati-Weierstrass theorem, Picard's theorem, residues.

IX. Cauchy's theorem: continuous logarithms, increments in the logarithm and argument along a curve, winding number, winding numbers of contours, separation lemma, Cauchy's theorem, homotopy and winding numbers, homotopy version of Cauchy's theorem, Runge's approximation theorem.

X. Further development of basic complex function: simply connected domains, winding number criterion, Cauchy's theorem for simply connected domains, existence of primitives, existence of logarithms, existence of harmonic conjugates, simple connectivity and homotopy, the residue theorem, Cauchy's formula, the argument principle, Rouche's theorem, the local mapping theorem, inverses, conformal equivalence, the Riemann mapping theorem, an extremal property of Riemann maps, Stieltjes-Osgood theorem.

In comparison with the first edition, the book contains two new sections: on division of power series and on homotopy. Moreover, the following four appendices have been added: 1.~Sufficient condition for differentiability. 2.~Two instances of the chain rule. 3.~Groups, and linear-fractional transformations. 4.~Differentiation under the integral sign.

The presented material is illustrated by various examples and exercises. The textbook may be recommended to everybody who, having some basic knowledge from real analysis, is willing to enter the world of complex analysis --- the book will guide him in a smooth way in this direction.

Real mathematical analysis

This book, in its second edition, provides the basic concepts of real analysis. The book is divided into six chapters. In Chapter 1, entitled Real numbers, the author presents Dedekind's method of constructing a real number, which shows that \(\mathbb{R}\), \([a,b]\) and \((a,b)\) are uncountable, \(\mathbb{N}\)\(\times\)\(\mathbb{N}\), \(\mathbb{Q}\), \(\mathbb Q^m \) are denumerable, offers Schroeder-Bernstein's theorem and gives some properties of continuous functions on an interval.

Chapter 2, entitled A taste of topology, deals with the metric space notions, continuity, the topology of a metric space, compactness, connectedness, coverings, Cantor sets and the construction of \(\mathbb{R}\) from \(\mathbb{Q}\) by completion.

Chapter 3, entitled Functions of a real variable, is dedicated to the notions of differentiation, Riemann integration, series of numbers and functions.

Chapter 4 -- Function spaces -- is about functions viewed en masse; uniform convergence and \(C^0[a, b]\), power series, compactness and equicontinuity in \(C^0\) (Arzela-Ascoli theorem, Heine-Borel theorem), uniform approximation in \( C^0 \) (Weierstrass approximation theorem, Stone-Weierstrass theorem), contractions and ODE's (Banach's contraction principle, Brouwer's theorem, Picard's theorem), analytic functions, nowhere differentiable continuous functions (Baire's theorem), the space of unbounded functions are studied.

Chapter 5 -- Multivariable calculus -- contains the natural geometric theory of calculus in \(n\) dimensions. Elements of linear algebra, derivatives, the mean value theorem, smoothness classes implicit and inverse functions, rank theorem, Lagrange multipliers, multiple integrals, Fubini's theorem, Cavalieri's principle, differential form, Stokes' formula, Poincaré's lemma, Brouwer's fixed point theorem are given.

Chapter 6 -- Lebesgue theory -- is dedicated to the geometric theory of Lebesgue measure and integration. Thus, the author covers the Lebesgue outer measure, affine motions, measurable product theorem, zero slice theorem, Lebesgue integrals, Cavalieri's principle, Fubini-Tonelli theorem, Vitali covering lemma, Lebesgue density theorem, Lebesgue's fundamental theorem of calculus, Lebesgue's last theorem.

The book contains a large number of over 520 exercises which were attentively chosen by the author. The exercises hold a high level of difficulty and cover a vast portion of mathematical analysis. The bibliography of the study contains 26 famous works from real mathematical analysis. Over 150 illustrations elucidate abstract concepts and salient points in proofs.

For the reviewer, it has been an exciting cover of this book. I strongly recommend it to everyone who wishes to study real mathematical analysis.

For the first edition see [Zbl 1003.26001].

First-order logic and automated theorem proving.

The second edition of this book is an update and a revision of its first edition (1990; Zbl 0692.68002). The book treats propositional logic, first-order logic and first-order logic with equality. For each of these, resolution and semantic tableau systems are presented as (refutation-based) proof procedures; also, soundness and completeness results of the theorem provers considered are established. Based on Robinson's unification algorithm, implementations of semantic tableaux in Prolog are given, and similar implementations of resolution procedures are outlined as projects. Additional proof procedures are specified, e.g., axiom systems (Hilbert systems), natural deduction, and Gentzen sequents. For each level of logic considered in this book, the necessary semantical background is considered: Boolean valuations in the propositional case, models in the first-order case, and normal models in the first-order case with equality. Additionally, various fundamental formal properties are derived, e.g., for first-order logic the replacement and skolemization Theorem, Herbrand's Theorem, Gentzen's Theorem, the cut elimination Theorem, Craig's interpolation Theorem, Beth's definability Theorem, and Lyndon's homomorphism Theorem. Throughout the book, a system of uniform notation is used (following Smullyan).

[For the entire collection see Zbl 0715.00021.]

Recent results closely related to the Knaster-Kuratowski-Mazurkiewicz theorem (KKM theorem) on closed coverings of a simplex are surveyed, in particular their interconnections are clarified. Fundamentals of real analysis

This book contains a complete course of real analysis. It begins with the set-theoretic foundations of modern mathematics and basic facts of general topology. In the next chapters readers can find the Lebesgue's theory of measure and integration including: convergence theorems, the fundamental theorem of calculus, product measures and iterated integrals, Radon-Nikodým theorem and Lebesgue decompositions of measures. A first course in analysis

This book is an excellent textbook on analysis from a well-known author. It is addressed to undergraduate students and will be useful for lecturers as well. The presentation is reader-friendly and a student reading it can feel as if the material is presented by the favorite teacher. The book is well-marked with accents: immediately it is clear if this is an important definition or theorem, or if it is a technical phrase. Most proofs of statements are completely clear and concise. The parts of proofs left as exercises to the reader require a careful study of the material.

The book is divided into nine chapters. Chapter 1, \textit{The real numbers}, is devoted to the basis of analysis (numbers, sets, countable and uncountable sets, open and closed sets, series, trigonometric functions, Cauchy sequences, continuous functions). Here, the first fundamental theorems are presented: the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem, the Cantor theorem, the extreme value theorem and the intermediate value theorem.

Chapter 2 is titled \textit{Differentiation}. Here, the author considers limits, derivatives, critical points and proves such theorems as the mean value theorem, L'Hopital's rule and Taylor's theorem.

Chapter 3, \textit{Integration}, presents the Riemann integral with all its important properties. The improper integral and the Riemann-Stieltjes integral are also considered in this chapter. Here, the author also introduces the logarithm and exponential functions, the fundamental theorem of calculus and Lebesgue's theorem on Riemann integrability are proven.

The small Chapter 4, \textit{Sequences of functions}, is devoted to the convergence of a sequence of functions: pointwise and uniform convergence. The Weierstrass M-test for power series is also presented.

From Chapter 5, \textit{Metric and Euclidean spaces}, on multivariable analysis begins. In this chapter, the topology of a \(p\)-dimensional Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^p\) is studied (completeness, separability, compactness and connectedness). The author proves the Cauchy-Schwarz-Bunyakovskiy inequality, the Heine-Borel theorem and Dini's theorem for continuous functions, the Stone-Weierstrass theorem and the Arzela-Ascoli theorem.

Chapter 6, \textit{Differentiation in higher dimension}, presents the concept of differentiability for functions of several variables. The author carefully introduces linear transformations and discusses tangent planes. The most important theorems in this chapter are the inverse function theorem and the implicit function theorem. Also, Lagrange multipliers is considered in this chapter.

Chapter 7 is devoted to \textit{Integration in higher dimension}. Here, the Riemann integral on Jordan sets is discussed. Fubini's theorem and the change of variables are cornerstones of this chapter.

The most difficult chapters for students are Chapters 8 and 9 titled as \textit{Curves and surfaces} and \textit{Differential forms}. Here, the author carefully deals with integration on regular curves, surfaces and more general on \(q\)-surfaces. The key theorems are Green's theorem, Gauss's theorem and Stokes's theorem as well as its generalization, the generalized Stokes's theorem.

In the course of the entire book, the author places in footnotes parts of the biographies of eminent mathematicians who created the analysis. It is also worth noting that, like any great work, this textbook is not devoid of some typos and inaccuracies that will be useful to attentive students who pay attention to them.

Distributional strategies for games with incomplete information

We study games with incomplete information from a point of view which emphasizes the empirical predictions arising from game-theoretic models. Using the notion of ``distributional'' strategies, we prove four main theorems: (i) a mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium existence theorem, (ii) a pure-strategy equilibrium existence theorem, (iii) a pure-strategy \(\epsilon\)-equilibrium existence theorem, and (iv) a theorem describing how the set of equilibria of a game varies with the parameters of the game.

The Atiyah-Singer index theorem

The Atiyah-Singer index theorem is a landmark achievement in 20th century which brings analysis, geometry and topology together. It computes the Fredholm index of the elliptic operators on compact manifolds, which is the dimension of the kernel minus the dimension of the cokernel, in terms of topological invariants of the operator and the underlying manifold. This theorem combines the Chern-Gauss-Bonnet theorem in differential geometry, the Hirzebruch-Riemann-Roch theorem in complex geometry and the Hirzebruch's signature theorem in topology and has numerous generalizations and implications in algebraic geometry, number theory, representation theory, operator algebras, nonlinear analysis and theoretical physics, etc. It reflects the philosophy to unify various different parts in mathematics.

This paper is a very good survey for the Atiyah-Singer index theorm, including some motivations and many implications of it. It is a tribute to Michael Atiyah. Naturaly it focuses on aspects of his work and his influence. A lecture based on this paper may be viewed at \url{https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AJHKp9kYm90}.

In Section 2, the author recalls the antecedents and motivations of the index theorem from algebraic geometry and topology, from the classical Riemann-Roch theorem, its higher dimensonal generalization by Hirzebruch, Hirzebruch's signature theorem to the Grothendieck's relative version of the Riemann-Roch theorem. These motivate Atiyah and his collaborators to introduce topological K-theory using Bott periodicity and to ask a question about why the \(\widehat{\mathrm{A}}\)-genus is an integer for a spin manifold.

Section 3 is dedicated to the antecedents of the index theorem in analysis, including de Rham theorem, Hodge theorem and Dolbeault theorem. The author also recalls some basic facts about Fredholm operators and the activity around Fredholm indices of elliptic operators during the years 1920--1963.

In Section 4, the author sketches the cobordism proof and the K-theory proof of the index theorem briefly and lists a few early applications of the index theorem. In particular, the integrality of the \(\widehat{\mathrm{A}}\)-genus about a spin manifold is explained as the index of the Dirac operator.

In Section 5, the author introduces various forms/generalizations of the index theorem. These include an equivariant index theorem, which is a generalization of the Lefchetz fixed point theorem, index theorems for compact manifolds with local boundary or the covering of compact manifolds and an index theorem for real elliptic operators, Clifford linear operators or a family of elliptic operators.

Section 6 is for the heat equation proof of the index theorem. This led to a local version of the index theorem. This work was completely in the early 1970s. In the 1980s, several new proofs of the local index theorem led to a deeper understanding of the index theory. The author summarizes these contributions by many mathematicians through various explanations of the mysterious \(\widehat{\mathrm{A}}\)-genus appearing in the index theorem.

Section 7 focuses on the geometric invariants of the Dirac operator, especially on the Atiyah-Patodi-Singer \(\eta\) invariant, whose definition is parallel to that of an \(L\)-function in analytic number theory. This \(\eta\) invariant is just the boundary term of the index theorem for a global boundary condition. It has many applications in differential K-theory and physics.

In Section 8, the author discusses the applications of the index theory in theoretical physics, mainly on the Atiyah's work in the late 1980s on anomalies and on his axiomatization of topological field theory.

Complex proofs of real theorems

This book is a nice collection of beautiful gems from various areas of mathematics, the simplest, the clearest and the most efficient proofs of which are the ones by complex variables. It is directed to specialists and graduate students familiar with the basics of analytic functions and complex analysis.

The first chapter, ``Early triumphs'', is devoted to two classical problems from the past. One of them is to find the sum of the series \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac1{n^{2k}}\), where \(k=1,2,\dots\). Its most famous case, \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac1{n^2}\), the so-called Basel problem, was solved by Euler in 1735. The solution presented by the authors is based on the residue theorem. A remarkably short proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra, which makes use of the Cauchy integral formula for circles, is given as well.

Chapter 2 deals with uniform approximation by weighted polynomials of \(C_0(\mathbb R)\)-functions. The authors discuss, among other things, the Müntz approximation theorem, providing necessary and sufficient conditions for a set of powers of the identity function to span the space \(C[0,1]\), and present Rudin's proof of it which is based on the Cauchy integral formula.

The third chapter, devoted to operator theory, starts with Rosenblum's elegant proof of the Fuglede-Putnam theorem for bounded normal operators on a complex Hilbert space, which makes use of Liouville's theorem in Banach spaces. Other topics include properties of Toeplitz operators on the space \(H^2\) on the unit circle, related to their indices and the winding numbers of their symbols; Halmos' elegant proof of Beurling's theorem about closed invariant subspaces of the unilateral shift operator on \(H^2\); Szegö's theorem in prediction theory; Thorin's proof of the Riesz convexity theorem about linear operators on pairs of \(L^p\) spaces, based on the three lines theorem; Young's inequality for convolution operators on \(L^p(\mathbb R)\) and the Hausdorff-Young theorem. The chapter concludes with various properties of the Hilbert transform of real-valued integrable functions on \(\mathbb R\), the proof of which is based on the Cauchy theorem.

In Chapter 4 the authors discuss various connections between complex and harmonic analysis. The chapter includes Newman's complex analytic proof of the uniqueness of the Fourier transforms; Lax's proof of the linearity of the solutions of the equations \(f(2x)=2f(x)\) and \(\frac1{x}\int_0^xf(y)dy=f(x/2)\); the uniqueness of the Radon transform; the Paley-Wiener theorem; the Titchmarsh convolution theorem about the supports of the convolutions of \(L^1(\mathbb R_{+})\)-functions. The chapter ends with the proof of Hardy's theorem on the connection of \(L^1(\mathbb R)\)-functions with their Fourier transforms, which utilizes the Phragmén-Lindelöf principle and Liouville's theorem.

Chapter 5 is devoted to the proof of the celebrated Gleason-Kahane-Zelazko theorem, which makes use of Liouville's theorem in Banach spaces. Namely, a linear subspace of codimension 1 in a commutative Banach algebra is a maximal ideal if and only if it contains no invertible elements, or, alternatively, a linear unital complex valued functional on a unital Banach algebra is multiplicative if and only if it does not vanish on invertible elements.

Chapter 6 deals with complex dynamics. The authors present here the proof of the famous Fatou-Julia-Baker theorem describing the Julia sets of rational functions of degree \(\geq 2\) and of transcendental entire functions as the closures of the function's repelling periodic points.

Newman's remarkable proof of the classical prime number theorem about the asymptotic growth of the set of prime numbers, and a simple proof of a theorem of Tauberian type for Laplace transforms, based again on the Cauchy integral formula, are presented in the last chapter.

Two non-standard applications of complex variables -- to supersonic fluid dynamics and to statistical mechanics -- are discussed briefly at the end.

The book concludes with several appendices, providing the necessary background, on Liouville's theorem in Banach spaces, the Borel-Carathéodory inequality, the Phragmén-Lindelöf theorem, Doetsch's three lines theorem -- a version of the classical three circle theorem of Hadamard, and the normal families of meromorphic functions, including Montel's theorem, Marty's theorem, and Zalcman's lemma.

Each chapter ends with useful comments, related results, alternative approaches, historical notes and references. The book is self-contained and very well written. The authors have done a marvelous job in collecting these topics and presenting them in an organized and transparent way. We can only agree with them that ``lovers of analysis and beautiful proofs will read and reread this slim volume with pleasure and profit.''

Two important theorems that are really one

Summary: An elementary proof of the equivalence of the intermediate value theorem and a fixed point theorem on the real line illustrates the equivalence of the Brouwer fixed point theorem and the Poincaré-Miranda theorem.

A note on Hamiltonian circuits

The purpose of this note is to prove the following Theorem 1. Let \(G\) be a graph with at least three vertices. If, for some \(s\), \(G\) is \(s\)-connected and contains no independent set of more than \(s\) vertices, then \(G\) has a Hamiltonian circuit. This theorem is sharp. For \(s\) relatively large with respect to the number of vertices of \(G\), our Theorem 1 follows from a stronger statement due to Nash-Williams and Bondy [\textit{C. St. J. A. Nash-Williams}, Studies pure Math., Papers presented to Richard Rado on the Occasion of his sixty-fifth Birthday, 157-183 (1971; Zbl 0223.05123), Lemma 4]. As an easy consequence of Theorem 1 we obtain Theorem 2. Let \(G\) be an \(s\)-connected graph with no independent set of \(s+2\) vertices. Then \(G\) has a Hamiltonian path. The technique used in the proof of Theorem 1 yields also Theorem 3. Let \(G\) be an \(s\)-connected graph containing no independnet set of \(s\) vertices. Then \(G\) is Hamiltonian-connected (i.e. every pair of vertices is joined by a Hamiltonian path).

Generic initial ideals

This is a semi-expository article (with many new proofs of known results) on generic initial ideals which began as course notes for a course given at UCLA (University of California, Los Angeles) and was later given as a series of lectures at the Recerca Matemática Summer School in Commutative Algebra during the summer of 1996 in Barcelona.

Besides the introduction, the article consists of six chapters: (1) The initial ideal; (2) Regularity and saturation; (3) The Macaulay-Gotzmann estimates on the growth of ideals, (4) Points in \(\mathbb{P}^2\) and curves in \(\mathbb{P}^3\), (5) Gins (``generic initial ideals'') in the exterior algebra; and (6) Lexicographic gins and partial elimination ideals.

Each chapter ends with some short comments for students. According to the author these notes are ``a strange brew of commutative algebra, geometry, and combinatorics, with a little bit of non-commutative algebra thrown in for good measure''. Some of the topics included are monomial ideals, gins, Galligo's theorem, Eliahou-Kervaire's theorem, Hilbert's syzygy theorem, the Bayer-Stillman theorem on the regularity of an ideal I, Macaulay's estimate on growth of ideals, the hyperplane restriction theorem, Gotzmann's persistence theorem, Gotzmann's regularity theorem, results of Ellia-Peskine and Gruson-Peskine, the Hilbert-Burch theorem, Laudal's lemma, Macaulay's bound for exterior ideals, and the Kruskal-Katona theorem.

Complex analysis

The book of the known mathematicians J. Bak and D. Newman is an excellent introduction into the theory of analytic functions of one complex variable. The book is written on an elementary level and so it supports students in the early stages of their mathematical studies. The content of the book deals with: complex numbers, power series, analyticity, Cauchy-Riemann equations, line Integral, entire functions, Liouville theorem, Gauss-Lucas theorem, mean-value theorem, maximum-modulus theorem, Schwarz' Lemma, Cauchy's theorem, Morera's theorem, isolated singularities of analytic functions, residue theorem, conformal mapping, Riemann mapping theorem, harmonic functions, analytic continuation, gamma function, zeta function, applications to other areas of mathematics. It has xii+328 pages throughout which the authors make all efforts to give as many results as possible, and yet provide lots of details to make the reading easier.

There are no lengthy discussions, no complicated proofs, and no dependence on other parts of mathematics, especially on topology. This is the reason why this book may be recommended especially to beginners in complex analysis. The book also contains many illustrations, examples and exercises, which give additional information and explanations. On the other hand, the authors point out many interesting applications in other mathematical areas, e.g., the prime number theorem and a variation problem.

Convexity in graphs and hypergraphs

The notion of convexity in graphs is extended to hypergraphs and analogues are obtained of several classical results including the Milman- Klein-Minkowski theorem, Caratheodory's theorem and Tietze's convexity theorem. New results on chordal graphs and hypergraphs are obtained.

The authors prove two main theorems. Each theorem is a generalization of the EGZ Theorem [\textit{P. Erdős}, \textit{A. Ginzburg} and \textit{A. Ziv}, Theorem in additive number theory, Bull. Res. Council Israel 10F, 41--43 (1961; Zbl 0063.00009)] as well as a generalization of a known theorem in Ramsey theory.

On the distribution of the singular values of Toeplitz matrices

The involved discussion is based on a theorem of Szegö concerning the asymptotic distribution of the eigenvalues of the Toeplitz matrices \(T_ n[f]\) where f(0) is a real-valued bounded measurable function which is periodic with period \(2\pi\). Simple examples show that a similar theorem for the case where f(0) is not real-valued is impossible. An interlacing problem for singular values is proved. The theorem, although of a more general nature than usual, has a proof which is essentially the proof of the interlacing theorem for Hermitian matrices. The theorem is applied to obtain extensions of the \textit{G. Szegö} theorem [Math. Zeitschr. 6, 167-202 (1920; JFM 47.0391.04)] to the singular values of \(T_ n[f]\) when f is not a real-valued function.

Simple proofs of classical theorems in discrete geometry via the Guth-Katz polynomial partitioning technique

The paper reproves some classical theorems of discrete geometry (the Szemerédi-Trotter theorem and the Pach-Sharir theorem bounding the number of incidences between points and lines, and the theorem of Chazelle and Welzl about spanning trees with low crossing number) using the Guth-Katz partitioning of finite point sets in a Euclidean space based on the Stone-Tukey ham-sandwich theorem. The proofs are self-contained and appropriate for teaching.

A fixed point theorem of Krasnoselskii-Schaefer type

The authors focus on three fixed point theorems and an integral equation. Schaefer's fixed point theorem yields a \(T\)-periodic solution of
\[
x(t)= a(t)+ \int^t_{t- h}D(t, s)g(s, x(s))ds\tag{1}
\]
if \(D\) and \(g\) satisfy certain sign conditions independent of their magnitude. A combination of the contraction mapping theorem and Schauder's theorem (known as Krasnoselskii's theorem) yields a \(T\)-periodic solution of
\[
x(t)= f(t, x(t))+ \int^t_{t- h}D(t,s)g(s, x(s))ds\tag{2}
\]
if \(f\) defines a contraction and if \(D\) and \(g\) are small enough.

The authors prove a fixed point theorem which is a combination of the contraction mapping theorem and Schaefer's theorem which yields a \(T\)-periodic solution of (2) when \(f\) defines a contraction mapping, while \(D\) and \(g\) satisfy the aforementioned sign conditions.

Some personal delights in geometry --- from earliest days to fractals

As the title indicates, this article is a sort of reminiscences of an ``admirer'' of geometry --- starting with very early days and ending with the age of fractals. Among the classical theorems reminisced are Pythagoras theorem (along with the proof as it appears in the `Elements' of Euclid), Ptolemy's theorem, Nine-point circle theorem, Feuerbach's theorem, Pascal's ``Mystic Hexagram'' theorem and Brianchon's theorem. The article ends with answering the question: What are fractals and why fractal geometry. Thirty six beautiful figures make the article more attractive.

Linearization of regular proper groupoids.

The author hopes eventually to establish a linearization theorem for all proper groupoids near their orbits, as was expressed in [\textit{A. Weinstein}, Lett. Math. Phys. 52, No. 1, 93--102 (2000; Zbl 0961.22004)]. Since the most general version would require a still unproven linearization theorem around fixed points, this paper is devoted to a proof of a somewhat restricted theorem claiming that, under a differential-topological finiteness assumption, the Lie groupoid is isomorphic to its linear approximation in some neighborhood of each orbit. The theorem follows from a slice theorem asserting that a linearization of the restriction to a slice extends to a linearization along an orbit.

On the loop- and sphere-theorem

This paper gives a new and unified proof of the loop theorem and sphere theorem (for 3-manifolds with a nonsphere boundary component) which were first proved by Papakyriakopoulos and are fundamental to the study of 3-manifolds. This proof makes no use of a tower construction, and does not even involve the resolution of self-intersections. It rather depends on minimizing, in the appropriate measure, the combinatorial area of appropriate singular surfaces.

Lectures on the Mordell-Weil theorem. Transl. and ed. by Martin Brown from notes by Michel Waldschmidt

These notes are based on a course given by J.-P. Serre at the Collège de France in 1980 and 1981. The notes provide an introduction to and summary of many of the major ideas and results in the theories of rational and integral points on algebraic varieties.

Beginning with a study of height functions, the book progresses to a proof of the weak Mordell-Weil theorem using the Chevalley-Weil theorem. After a brief discussion of descent arguments the full Mordell-Weil theorem is proved.

Following this is a description of Mordell's conjecture, and a discussion of the major results (Chabauty's theorem, the Manin-Demyanenko theorem, Mumford's theorem) and applications that preceded Faltings' proof. - Integral points and quasi-integral points on curves are studied via Siegel's theorem and Baker's method. The study includes a discussion of effectivity, and applications to the arithmetic of curves.

The problem of lifting rational points under morphisms is introduced with the notion of thin sets and Hilbert's irreducibility theorem. Applications to the construction of Galois extensions with certain prescribed Galois groups, and to the construction of elliptic curves of large rank are given. There is also a discussion of the large sieve, and applications to the study of thin sets.

Finally, an appendix contains some remarks about the class number 1 problem, and connections with elliptic and modular curves.

Summary: The aim of this note is to point out that the Ionescu Tulcea and Marinescu theorem can be reinforced, using a Nussbaum formula for the essential spectral radius of an operator. As an application to probability theory, a large deviation theorem is proved.

Generalized quasiconvexities, cone saddle points, and minimax theorem for vector-valued functions

This paper gives (1) an existence theorem for weak type generalized saddle points; (2) an existence theorem for strong type generalized saddle points and (3) a generalized minimax theorem for a vector-valued function. These theorems are generalizations of the author's recent results. Some new concepts of convexity and continuity of vector-valued functions are introduced for such generalizations. The compression theorem II: directed embeddings

This is the second of a set of three papers on the compression theorem. It contains a geometric proof of the normal deformation theorem, which is a general version of the compression theorem and was proved in the first paper of the series [Geom. Topol. 5, 399-429 (2001; Zbl 1002.57057)] by different methods. Central step in the present proof is a flattening lemma. It states that a compressible manifold \(M^n \subset Q^q \times {\mathbb{R}}^t\), \( q - n \geq 1\), may be deformed by a \(C^0\)-small isotopy in Q in a position, such that its tangent space lies in a given neighborhood of the horizontal subset of the Grassmann bundle of n-planes in the tangent bundle \(T(Q^q \times {\mathbb{R}}^t)\). Gromov's theorem on directed embeddings [\textit{M. Gromov}, Partial differential relations (Springer-Verlag, Berlin), (1986; Zbl 0651.53001)] is deduced from the normal deformation theorem. It is remarked that the normal deformation theorem may be deduced from Gromov's theorem.

A course on topological groups

The aim of the book is a self-contained proof of the Peter-Weyl theorem. The author follows the classical approach and gradually builds all necessary topological, analytical and algebraic ingredients. After a very brief introduction to topological spaces and topological groups in Chapter 1, Haar measure and \(L^1\)-algebras of locally compact groups are discussed in Chapter 2, while Chapter 3 is dedicated to Hilbert spaces and the spectral theorem. The last Chapter 4 contains the proof of Peter-Weyl's theorem and its connection to the Bohr's theorem on almost periodic functions. No further applications are given, in particular no connection to the Pontryagin duality theorem is mentioned at all.

Security markets. Stochastic models

This book presents the theory of allocation and pricing of ``financial securities in competitive markets with symmetrically informed agents. The intended audience includes researchers and graduate students interested in the economic theory of security markets''. The author has attempted a mathematically self-contained presentation and his book underscores the mathematical sophistication that underlies modern economic theory. The presentation relies on

(1) elementary functional analysis including a discussion of the Hahn- Banach theorem, the \(weak\)-\({}^*\)-topology on the space of measures, the Riesz representation theorem for Hilbert spaces and the Krein-Rutman theorem for the extension of positive, continuous, linear functions on ordered normed vector spaces;

(2) optimization theory in infinite-dimensional spaces including a discussion of the Kuhn-Tucker theorem;

(3) dynamic programming including Blackwell's theorem and the Bellman operator;

(4) probability theory including Lindeberg's central limit theorem and Donsker's theorem;

(5) fixed point theory including the Fan-Glicksberg theorem for locally convex vector spaces and the Banach fixed point theorem for contractions;

(6) stochastic processes and stochastic integration including Girsanov's theorem for semi-martingales and the Kunita-Watanabe inequality.

All of this mathematics is interlaced with the economics and together they span four chapters spread over 350 pages. The first introduces static markets and the second extends this to stochastic economies. The last two chapters are devoted to models of asset pricing, the first covering discrete time and the second, continuous time. Almost all sections have exercises and bibliographic notes. This is a clearly written and useful book for students and researchers in both economics and applied mathematics but a reader without a solid grounding in one or the other of the subjects might well find it somewhat dizzying.

On Cartan's theorem and Cartan's conjecture

The author gives a mild generalisation of Cartan's theorem on the value distribution for a holomorphic curve in projective space relative to hyperplanes. The point is that, via the author's dictionary with number theory [Lect. Notes Math. 1239 (1987; Zbl 0609.14011), Chapter 3], Cartan's theorem is almost equivalent to Schmidt's subspace theorem. The present improvement both yields a simpler proof and a stronger version of Cartan's theorem, in particular permitting the author to correct, and thus complete, his `A refinement of Schmidt's subspace theorem' [Am. J. Math. 111, 489-518 (1989; Zbl 0662.14002)].

Minimal edge-coverings of pairs of sets

Total dual integrality from directed graphs, crossing families, and sub- and supermodular functions

[For the entire collection see Zbl 0535.00030.]

This paper surveys old and new results asserting the total dual integrality of certain systems of linear inequalities, involving directed graphs, crossing families, and sub- and supermodular functions. The basis is a proof technique set up by Edmonds, Giles, Hoffman, Johnson, Lovász and Robertson of first showing that the active constraints in the optimum of the linear program can be chosen to be ''nice'' (e.g. ''cross-free'' or ''laminar''), and next that nice constraint sets are unimodular. This implies that the linear programs have integer optimum solutions.

The results discussed are König's matching and covering theorems, Menger's theorem, Ford-Fulkerson's max-flow min-cut theorem, Dilworth's decomposition theorem for partially ordered sets, theorems on shortest paths, common SDR's and trees, Fulkerson's optimum branching theorem, the Lucchesi-Younger theorem, Nash-Williams' orientation theorem, Edmond's theorems on (poly)matroids and their intersection, extensions of these theorems to submodular flows by Edmonds, Giles, Frank, Tardos, Hoffman's theory of lattice polyhedra, Grishuhin's model, König's edge-colouring theorem, the Hoffman-Schwartz chain model, Edmonds' branching packing theorem, and results by the author on crossing families, strong connectors and supermodular colourings. A study is made of the interrelations between these results.

A note on Mikusiński's proof of the Titchmarsh convolution theorem

The Titchmarsh theorem was obtained by him in 1926 and it reads: Let \(f=f(t)\) and \(g=g(t)\) be complex-valued continuous functions on \([0,\infty)\). Then \(f\cdot g(t)=\int^{t}_{0}f(t-u)g(u)du\equiv 0\) implies f(t)\(\equiv 0\) or g(t)\(\equiv 0\). The original proof is not easy since it involves deap theorems in analytic function theory. An elementary proof was given in 1951 by J. Mikusiński. Although elementary, it is of 8 pages long. The purpose of this note is to modify Mikusinski's proof so that to obtain a plain proof of 3 pages long by making use of Liouville's theorem in analytic function theory and Weierstrass' polynomial approximation theorem. Thus starting from the special case \(f=g\), i.e., from \(\int^{t}_{0}f(t-u)f(u)du\equiv 0\) we get, for any T with \(0<T<\infty\), that there exists an M such that \(| \int^{T}_{-T}e^{zu}f(T-u)du| \leq M<\infty\) whenever Re \(z\geq 0\). This implies the existence of an N such that \(| \int^{T}_{0}e^{zu}f(T-u)du| \leq N<\infty\) for all complex number z, and hence, by Liouville's theorem \(\int^{T}_{0}e^{zu}f(T- u)du\equiv a\) constant. Thus, by differentiation at \(z=0\), we get \(\int^{T}_{0}u^ nf(T-u)du=0 (n=1,2,...)\), and so we obtain f(T- u)\(\equiv 0\) by virtue of the Weierstrass theorem. For the general case \(f\neq g\), this note makes use of the special case \(f=g\) result and an argument given by Mikusiński.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 0523.00008].

Semistable minimal models of threefolds in positive or mixed characteristic

In contrast with the classification theory of algebraic surfaces (which is characteristic free), the minimal model theory of algebraic threefolds is only completed over the field of characteristic 0, because the vanishing theorem of Kodaira type is necessary in the course of the proof. The purpose of this paper is to extend the minimal model theory to the positive or mixed characteristic case for 3-dimensional schemes which have semistable reduction over the spectrum of a Dedekind ring. By definition, such a 3-fold is fibered by a family of surfaces. From this, and by using known results on log surfaces, the author proves the cone theorem for these 3-folds (theorem 1.3). Then after proving weaker vanishing theorems (lemmas 2.1, 2.2), he proves the contraction theorem (theorem 2.3). After necessary additional assumptions, he proves also the termination of the sequence of flips (theorem 5.2), and the flip theorem (theorem 5.5). Now, the combination of the cone, the contraction, and the flip theorems, yields the main theorem of the paper: The minimal model theorem (theorem 5.7):

The given morphism has a birational model which is minimal or has a Mori fiber space structure.

Variations on Poincaré-Miranda's theorem

Poincaré-Miranda's theorem states that any continuous mapping from a parallelotope in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) into \(\mathbb{R}^n\), whose \(j\)th component takes constant opposite signs on the corresponding opposite \(j\)th-faces of the parallelotope (\(j=1,\dots, n\)), has at least one zero in this parallelotope. However this theorem does not hold on arbitrary infinite-dimensional parallelotopes.

In this work the author gives a simple analytical proof of Poincaré-Miranda's theorem as well as applying it to prove its geometric version due to Hurewicz. Finally he discusses the possibility of extending Poincaré-Miranda's theorem to infinite-dimensional spaces and proves the Poincaré-Miranda theorem on the Hilbert cube in \(l^2\).

Sz. Nagy, (d) the commutant lifting theorem with applications to problems of interpolation.

On the cohomology of finite soluble groups.

In this paper, a theorem of \textit{C. Parker} and \textit{P. Rowley} [Bull. Lond. Math. Soc. 42, No. 3, 417-419 (2010; Zbl 1193.20019)] is revisited and two vanishing theorems (Theorems 1 and 3) for group cohomology at dimensions 1 and 2 are proved. The author remarks that the vanishing theorem at dimension 1 is what is behind the Parker-Rowley theorem. Finally, some applications of these theorems are given.

If \(\Omega\) is a set of unary operations on a group \(G\), then \(\mathrm{comp}_\Omega(G)\) denotes the set of isomorphism classes of \(\Omega\)-composition factors of \(G\). The Parker-Rowley theorem states the following: Suppose that \(N\) is a nilpotent normal subgroup of a finite solvable group \(G\) such that \(\mathrm{comp}_G(G/N)\cap\mathrm{comp}_G(N)\) is empty. If \(H\) and \(K\) are subgroups of \(G\) such that \(HN=KN=G\) and \(H\cap N=K\cap N\), then \(H\) and \(K\) are conjugate in \(G\).

Motivated by this theorem, the following cohomological vanishing theorem is proved: Theorem 1. Let \(Q\) be a finite group and \(A\) be a finite \(Q\)-module. Assume that \(Q\) is \(p\)-solvable for all the primes \(p\) dividing the order of \(A\), and that \(\mathrm{comp}_Q(Q)\cap\mathrm{comp}_Q(A)\) is empty. Then \(H^1(Q,A)=0\).

Using this theorem, a generalization of the Parker-Rowley theorem is also given (Theorem 2). Then in Section 3, a similar vanishing result for group cohomology at dimension 2 is proved (Theorem 3). The assumptions of Theorem 3 are too technical to state here. The paper ends with some applications of these theorems to the splitting of group extensions and to the structure of automorphism groups of finite solvable groups with nilpotent length at most \(3\).

Existence of global weak solutions to compressible isentropic finitely extensible bead-spring chain models for dilute polymers

The purpose of this paper is to study the compressible Navier-Stokes-Fokker-Planck equation equation in non-dimensional form, with an elastic extra-stress tensor. The meanings of the constants and the Kramer's expression are described in detail. The main theorem characterizes the existence of a globally weak solution with given initial conditions. The proof uses a formal energy identity, Gronvalls inequality, Schauder's fixed point theorem, Lebesgue interpolation, Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality, generalized Korn's inequality, Sobolev embedding, Aubin-Lions-Simon compactness theorem, integration by parts, Lax-Milgram theorem, dominated convergence theorem, Poincaré inequality, Egoroff's theorem, Vitali's convergence therem, Dubinski's compactness theorem, Lipschitz continuity, Fatou's lemma, Dunford-Pettis therem, Hölder's inequality, Youngs function, Du Bois-Reymond's lemma, Bogovsky operator, Parseval-Plancherel formula, Riesz operator, Friedrichs mollifier.

A uniqueness theorem for an inverse electromagnetic scattering problem in inhomogeneous anisotropic media.

The authors formulate the direct scattering problem for electromagnetic waves as a boundary-value problem. The uniqueness theorem for this problem is formulated and proved, as well as the regularity theorem. The interior transmission problem is investigated, and the uniqueness theorem is proved for it as well. The results obtained for both problems serve to prove the uniqueness theorem for the inverse scattering problem.

On the zone theorem for hyperplane arrangements

In the last years many interesting papers about problems of computational geometry deal with arrangements of hyperplanes in \(d\)-dimensional real space. The known zone theorem says that the number of faces bounding the cells intersected by another hyperplane is \(O(n^{d-1})\). An irreparable error in the original proof of this theorem for \(d\geq 3\) has great significance, because the theorem is basic for fundamental algorithms and combinatorial applications. The authors present a correct inductive proof of the general zone theorem and a generalization of the theorem of pseudohyperplane arrangements. In the appendix a saved version of the original sweep proof for a partial case is discussed.

An elementary proof of the local central limit theorem

The authors give a proof (characteristic functions free) of the local central limit theorem for independent non-identically distributed integer valued random variables. The first theorem is formulated for the sum of \(n\) random variables. This theorem is restated for the triangular arrays of variables. The theorems have some interesting consequences. The vector-variable analog of the second theorem is also proved for an array of independent \(L\)-valued random vectors. \(L\) denotes the \(d\)-dimensional integer lattice.

Measures and integrals

This book is designed as an introductory and self-contained text in Lebesgue measure theory to the average mathematical undergraduate. The author's main aim is to give the differentiation theory for real functions of a real variable related to Lebesgue measure theory (that is, Lebesgue differentiation theorem derived from Vitali covering theorem), which is developed instructively and intelligibly in Chapter 5, and many useful examples related to this topic are included. His treatment of measure theory follows traditional order. That is, Chapter 1 concerns the history of the development from Riemann integral to Lebesgue integral. In Chapter 2, the theory of Lebesgue measure is developed by Carathéodory's method of extension and non Lebesgue-measurable set is also referred. Chapter 3 deals with the theory of measurable functions. In Chapter 4, Lebesgue integral is defined and some convergence theorems are obtained, making use of Fatou's lemma. Chapter 6 treats product measures and Fubini's theorem. In final Chapter 7, the theory of signed measures is studied, especially Radon-Nikodým theorem, Vitali-Hahn-Saks theorem and Lebesgue density theorem are discussed.

The Ahlswede-Daykin theorem

Summary: In Z. Wahrscheinlichkeitstheor. Verw. Geb. 43, 183-185 (1978; Zbl 0369.04004), \textit{Rudolf Ahlswede} and \textit{David Daykin} published a theorem which says that a certain inequality on nonnegative real-valued functions for pairs of points in a finite distributive lattice extends additively to pairs of lattice subsets. It is an elegant theorem with widespread applications to inequalities for systems of subsets, linear extensions of partially ordered sets, and probabilistic correlation. We review the theorem and its applications, and describe a recent generalization to \(n\)-tuples of points and subsets in distributive lattices. Although many implications of the Ahlswede-Daykin theorem follow from the weaker hypotheses of the widely-cited FKG theorem, several important implications are noted to require the stronger hypotheses of the basic theorem of Ahlswede and Daykin.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 0933.00056].

Minimally generated Boolean algebras

A Boolean algebra is minimally generated iff it is the union of a continuous well-ordered chain of subalgebras, where each \(B_{\alpha +1}\) is minimally generated over \(B_{\alpha}\). This paper proves basic theorems about minimally generated algebras. For example:

Theorem. Interval algebras and superatomic algebras are minimally generated.

Theorem. Minimally generated algebras are closed under product, homomorphic image, and products of finitely many factors.

Theorem. Every minimally generated algebra is co-absolute with an interval algebra.

Theorem. A minimally generated algebra cannot have an uncountable free subalgebra.

Sequences and series in Banach spaces

This remarkable book is devoted to some common geometrical properties of Banach spaces. The main results presented in this book were obtained during the last 15-20 years and described in different short and long articles strewn in numerous magazines till now and in essential they were unknown to many analysts. The book proposed to the reader aims to make this results accesible to him; it is written in a lively and informal manner and not burdened with technical and specifical jargon. Most readers of this book can find many interesting new results and use them in their usual mathematical activity.

Here is a list of topics presented in the book: 1. Riesz's lemma and compactness in Banach spaces (including Rottman's separation theorem); 2. The weak and \(weak^*\) topologies (in particular Mazur's theorem on closure of convex sets and Goldstine's and Alaoglu's theorems); 3. The Eberlein-Šmulian theorem; 4. The Orlicz-Pettis theorem; 5. Basic sequences (including Mazur's technique, the Bessaga-Pelczynski selection principle); 6. The Dvoretsky-Rogers theorem; 7. The classical Banach spaces (the space \(C(\Omega)\) of continuous functions on \(\Omega\), the special properties of the spaces \(c_ 0,\ell_ 1,\ell_{\infty}\), the spaces c\(a(\Sigma)\) and \(L_ 1(\mu)\) and at last the spaces \(L_ p[0,1] (1\leq p<\infty))\); 8. Weak convergence and unconditionally convergent series in uniformly convex spaces; 9. Extremal tests for weak convergence of sequences and series (Rainwater's and Elton's theorems); 10. Grothendieck's inequality and the Grothendieck-Lindenstrauss-Pelczynski cycle of ideas; 11. Ramsey's theorem; 12. Rosenthal's \(\ell_ 1\) theorem; 12. The Josefson-Nissenzweig theorem; 13. Banach spaces with \(weak^*\) sequentially compact dual balls; 14. The Elton-Odell \((1+\epsilon)\)-separation theorem. Every small chapter devoted to single topics contains numerous interesting exercises and notes and remarks complementing the main text essentially.

Some recent problems in combinatorial mathematics

The author presents a brief survey of recent problems in combinatorial mathematics. He first mentions that the theory of flows in networks developed by Ford and Fulkerson provides procedures for dealing with a variety of combinatorial problems, e.g., Gale's supply demand theorem, Hoffman's circulation theorem, Menger's theorem in graph theory, Hall's theorem on systems of distinct representatives and the structure of \((0,1)\) matrices with specified rows and column sums. Among other recent developments are mentioned the author's work on minimal and maximal traces and maximal term ranks of a class of \((0,1)\) matrices, inequalities for permanents of doubly stochastic matrices and \((0,1)\) matrices, theorem of Bose, Shrikhande, and Parker [\textit{R. C. Bose}, \textit{S. S. Shrikhande}, and \textit{E. T. Parker}, Can. J. Math. 12, 189--203 (1960; Zbl 0093.31905)] regarding the existence of a pair of orthogonal Latin squares, Bruck-Ryser theorem,on the non existence of finite projective planes and the existence problem in the study of Hadamard matrices.

A general atomic decomposition theorem and Banach's closed range theorem

Banach's closed range theorem is proved by using a general atomic decomposition theorem for a Banach space. This theorem can be found in an earlier paper of the author [Quart. J. Math., Oxford II. Ser 37, 129-136 (1986; Zbl 0594.46019)], however a reformulation and a new proof is given in the present note.

Errata: Harmonically weighted Dirichlet spaces associated with finitely atomic measures
